title: Agent's Take: Brandon Aiyuk has only himself to blame for 49ers limbo chaos
summary: The wide receiver remains tied to San Francisco through the reserve/left squad list, and his refusal to seek reinstatement has kept his NFL future frozen
full_text:
The San Francisco 49ers report to training camp this weekend, and wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk is still under contract. Aiyuk's situation is one of the most bizarre in the salary cap era. He has nobody to blame but himself for his predicament.
The 2023 second team All-Pro's situation with the 49ers reached a point of no return last December when he was placed on the reserve/left squad list after going AWOL. It is rare for a team to put a player on the reserve/left squad list.
In order to be placed on the reserve/left squad list, a team must send a player who has left a letter warning him that he can be put on this list if he doesn't return within five days of his departure (i.e., a five-day letter). The player is prevented from playing for the rest of the season and isn't paid either once placed on this list. The player's contract also tolls, where it is frozen until he resumes playing.
Players on reserve/left squad are deemed retired, according to the NFL constitution and bylaws. A retired player must apply to the commissioner for reinstatement where his last team retains his contractual rights.
Aiyuk likely would have been promptly released by applying for reinstatement at any time during the offseason workout program. The 49ers wouldn't have wanted to be on the hook for $26.15 million of his $27 million 2026 salary if he got hurt on their watch. Had Aiyuk taken this approach, he probably would be with another team, eager to prove that there aren't any ill effects from tearing the ACL, MCL and meniscus.
Aiyuk chose to spend his time posting videos and messages on social media rather than taking constructive steps to accelerate his departure from the 49ers. It is believed that Aiyuk still hasn't started the reinstatement process. He has vowed that he will never set foot in the 49ers' facility.
"I will not be reinstating with [the 49ers] nor doing any kind of business with them," Aiyuk said via 49ers Web Zone recently. That's probably going to be a necessity for Aiyuk to resume his NFL career.
Aiyuk took a scorched-earth approach with his social media posts. He is playing the victim and isn't taking any responsibility for his circumstances.
Aiyuk revealed that he rehabbed his knee injury away from the 49ers, which wasn't their preference, and didn't stay in contact with the team during the process. This set the stage for the beginning of the end of Aiyuk's tenure in San Francisco. Under the NFL's collective bargaining agreement, injured players may be required to report to training camp up to five days before the mandatory reporting date for veterans. Given Aiyuk's rehab choices, he should have expected the 49ers to exercise this right.
The 49ers voided the $27 million in 2026 salary guarantees late last July in the four-year, $120 million contract extension Aiyuk signed at the end of August 2024. Contract guarantees are typically voided for an exhaustive list of defaults by a player. Aiyuk has the exact same default language in his contract as All-Pro edge rusher Nick Bosa and Pro Bowl quarterback Brock Purdy .
The most logical explanation is that the voiding resulted from Aiyuk breaching his contract by refusing to show up to training camp early, as required, due to his injury. The 49ers certainly aren't the only NFL team that would have taken this course of action if in those same shoes. Aiyuk also incurred a mandatory $50,000 fine for each day of training camp he missed.
The 49ers already had buyer's remorse about giving Aiyuk a contract extension after contentious negotiations in which he requested a trade and was a training camp hold in. Aiyuk was reportedly put on the trading block at the beginning of the 2025 offseason, but there was a soft trade market because of his knee injury.
Curiously, Aiyuk informed the NFLPA that he didn't want to fight the voiding of his guarantees. Aiyuk alleges that the NFLPA has engaged in a smear campaign to tarnish his image.
It's the NFLPA's job to protect players' rights. The NFLPA will routinely file a grievance on behalf of a player when a team voids salary guarantees, including cases where there isn't a great likelihood of prevailing. Knowing the NFLPA is going to fight can deter teams from overreaching in the future.
Aiyuk blamed his former agent, Athletes First's Ryan Williams, for his problems with the 49ers during the latter part of June. Williams also represents 49ers general manager John Lynch. He was Lynch's marketing agent during his playing career.
Representing a player and a general manager on the same team can be viewed as a conflict of interest. It's permissible under the NFLPA's agent regulations. The agent is required to disclose to the player, in writing, the NFL coaches and front-office personnel he also represents, in an addendum to the representation agreements of players he signs.
Aiyuk claimed he fired Williams in November. Williams was still listed as Aiyuk's agent of record by the NFLPA until the end of June, when Aiyuk sent a written notice as required by their agent regulations. Presumably, Aiyuk told Williams verbally last November that his services were no longer needed. Although Williams hadn't received a termination letter, it's understandable that he wouldn't be trying to protect Aiyuk's interest anymore after such a conversation.
There wasn't anything preventing Williams from making the split official at any time by sending Aiyuk a termination letter. For example, Antonio Brown and Johnny Manziel were fired by their respective agents.
I don't doubt that Aiyuk was told by the NFLPA and/or Williams that he would be released in early June at the latest. That was likely before Aiyuk went AWOL. The 49ers are less inclined to reward what can reasonably be viewed as negative behavior.
It would be in Aiyuk's best interest to get a new agent. At the very least, he should hire a former team executive for a flat fee or on an hourly basis, because his approach on his own is counterproductive.
A new agent or the team executive would surely give Aiyuk the same advice. He needs to apply for reinstatement to get off the reserve/left squad list and show up for training camp. Until Aiyuk does, he will remain in football limbo. The 49ers can effectively squat on his rights where he won't be paid, including a $24.935 million option bonus due Sept. 1 for a fake/dummy 2030 contract year since his contract continues to be tolled. As soon as Aiyuk reports to the 49ers, he will probably be released within the next 24 hours to avoid the payment, since the money is unsecured.
Aiyuk has openly campaigned to play for the Washington Commanders . He just announced on social media that he purchased a home in Northern Virginia for $10 million. That may no longer be an option. Aiyuk appears to have burned a bridge with Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels , who has been a close friend since their playing days together at Arizona State in 2019, and his mother. It's conceivable that Aiyuk and Daniels were trolling the public or have quietly made up behind the scenes.
Aiyuk's eagerness to play specifically for one team and his social media antics have undermined his contract leverage. His best-case scenario, considering his injury, if he had been acting more professionally, probably would have been a one-year contract similar to Odell Beckham Jr.'s in 2023 after missing the entire 2022 season recovering from tearing the ACL in his left knee for a second time during Super Bowl LVI. Beckham signed a one-year, $15 million contract worth up to $18 million through incentives with the Baltimore Ravens .
It wouldn't be surprising for Aiyuk to sign an incentive-laden one-year deal at or near his $1.215 million league minimum salary. Of course, that's predicated on Aiyuk getting reinstated. There is some speculation that Aiyuk's social media posts have raised enough red flags to deter any team from signing him.
Sometimes, silence is golden. Aiyuk should start taking that notion to heart if he's truly interested in…

title: Cardinals DC Nick Rallis up next: His presser
summary: The Arizona Cardinals are in full swing training camp mode. With a new head coach, a new OC, and a new special teams coordinator, most of the main coaching jobs came from somewhere else. Except for DC Nick Rallis. Head coach Mike LaFleur liked his style and defensive scheme, and he has been with the […]
full_text: Arizona Cardinals defensive coordinator Nick Rallis speaks with the media during training camp at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, on July 25, 2026. | Joe Rondone/The Republic / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Arizona Cardinals are in full swing training camp mode. With a new head coach, a new OC, and a new special teams coordinator, most of the main coaching jobs came from somewhere else. Except for DC Nick Rallis. Head coach Mike LaFleur liked his style and defensive scheme, and he has been with the club for three seasons. Usually, a new head man will bring in guys he has worked with in the past along the trail somewhere, but LaFleur and Rallis have never crossed paths. RELATED: OC NATHANIEL HACKETT OPENS UP Now that officially training camp has begun, Rallis is able to see the new guys a bit more and try to get a feel for where each player is at. There will be quite a few positions up for grabs, but thankfully, most positions will carry over the starter from last year. While the new offense is the talk of camp, Rallis’ group will need to step up this year. They were ranked the #27 defense overall last year. That breakdown is being ranked #24 in pass defense with 31 passing TDs and an average of 230.8 passing yards a game. They were #25 against the run, with an average of 126.9 rushing yards a game and allowed 19 rushing touchdowns. Rallis had his first training camp press conference. Here is what he said: ————————————————————————————- Q: How’s it been so far? How’s the start been? Rallis: It’s been good. Like you’d expect things to correct. I love the things that we can control, which is our attitude, our energy, our effort, and our focus levels. Those have been on point, and they’ve got to maintain that way, right? That’s easy to do for the first couple of days. You’ve got to be consistent with that. But I’ve been pleased. Q: We heard from BJ (Ojulari) yesterday, and just kind of his journey throughout his NFL career has been pretty tumultuous. What do you make of his resilience and where he’s at, his growth and what you expect from him this year? Rallis: People in this game, when you suffer an injury, you have to be resilient. And it’s hard. You just name it what it is. Like it’s really hard. Sometimes it can be depressing even during that time when you’re not able to be out on the field because you work so hard for those moments. You’ve got to look at this as growth to say that I can overcome adversity. And what’s exciting about BJ is he looks really good right now. He looks like a guy that’s put in a lot of work to get back to the player that he is. Things to continue to get better at, obviously. But it’s good to have him back out there full go and letting it loose. Q: And now that he’s fully healthy, what parts of his game are you seeing that’s reminding you, oh yeah, I remember this is who he was? Rallis: He’s got so much elusiveness off the edge. The thing I’m excited about when we get into pads is him setting those edges cuz I thought he’s done a really good job of that. He’s picked right back up from when he was feeling his best. That’s the BJ you see out there right now. Q: Coming back from an injury as well, he looked pretty explosive just in drills. What have you seen? Rallis: I saw the same thing. Obviously, as we get going, there’ll be things that he’s got an improvement plan that he can correct certain things. I know he’s got it on his mind cuz he was talking to me about it yesterday. Take it day by day. I know he’s a really good player, and so excited to have him back out there. Q: Max (Melton) had a nice pass breakup yesterday, and you guys have so many corners battling for time and spots on the depth chart. He has a lot of expectations because of where he was drafted. Where is he mentally? Like what is your kind of outlook on where he is? Rallis: He’s in a great spot. I think he took even a step from Day 1 to Day 2, going back to the offseason program, certain things that he needed to improve on. You saw him make some huge strides. I think he’s continuing to just develop his knowledge of the game and have some accelerated thinking based on what the offense is presenting before the snap. He’s in a phenomenal spot. And as you said, the whole room, it’s a great problem to have cuz you got so many guys that can go out there and play winning NFL football. It’s very competitive right now, which is what you want for that cornerback competition opposite Will (Johnson). What can make those guys stand out, because as you said, it’s a deep group. What can make those guys stand out in that competition? Everyone’s in competition right now across the whole roster. From the cornerback specifically number one to the cover guys. To me, like a premier guy at that spot can take away the best; there’s always going to be schematic things that, when you play a really good receiver. You’ll be dedicating numbers to him, but at the end of the day, there’s going to be one-on-ones throughout the game. And there’s going to be stressful downs for those guys. Can they go and win those downs? They’re not going to win all of them. To me, it’s the hardest position in football besides quarterback. Just because there are so many good receivers across this league, and you can be on an island out there with space. If you can deny the ball when you’re in a one-on-one matchup, to me, that’s everything. From there, like no matter what position, are you executing at a consistent level? Do you have a playing style, and can you take the ball away? Q: How is Starling (Thomas) looking and how does he fit into that conversation? Rallis: He’s right in there. He’s looked really good. He has worked very hard to get back to Himself, and there’s probably some rust he still needs to knock off. We’re only two days in, but you could just see he made a play yesterday, and the response from his teammates. I think says a lot about who he is to this team. Q; Another guy, Elijah Jones, had a couple of those plays yesterday. What kind of growth have you seen out of him? Rallis: Major growth. I think that the biggest growth I saw was in the offseason program. You just saw a comfort level. What I love about his game right now is he doesn’t get sped up. So, what I mean by that is, off of his releases or whether he’s playing off, just those first five yards are pivotal for a corner to be in good position throughout the down. And he has multiple ways that he can get up there and press right now that he’s very comfortable with. And he just never finds himself sped up later in the down. And then from there, like if you’re in a good position, he’s got length, he’s got speed, he’s got ability to disrupt the football, and let it loose. Excited where he’s trending. Q: How has Sean (Murphy-Bunting) adjusted? Rallis: He needed that time in the offseason program. Because he hadn’t been at a nickel, besides back when he was in Tampa and that was, selectively. You can just see like a comfort level right now, and we ask our nickels to do a lot, and so I’m not just even talking about playing that nickel spot. He’s playing deep zones and doing everything, and he’s taken a huge step. And he knows that. He’s made some big plays so far in two days. Q: When you have him wrap it and then whenever Garrett (Williams) comes back, how do you kind of decide? What are you looking for between those three in terms of just nickel? Rallis: We’ll assess that day by day. In terms of the nickel spot, it can depend on the situation and the package we’re in. If those guys can all help us win, they’re all going to play for us this year. Everybody in that back end. Q: How much of a physicality jump is that to go from outside to inside? Rallis: Situationally. It depends on how you match nickel. If you’re matching it versus bigger groups, a lot of times they do get down there in the box, and that’s where you’re going to see a little bit more physicality happening. Even in 11 personnel, if they are on the slot depends on…

title: Cardinals OC Nathaniel Hackett opens up
summary: Now that Arizona Cardinals training camp has begun, even if this stage is just helmets and shorts, the new offensive system is being explained and explained again to everyone on this year’s roster. A lot of new players can sometimes be a good thing.   RELATED: CARSON BECK SIGNS ROOKIE CONTRACT Offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett […]
full_text: Nathaniel Hackett (offensive coordinator) answers questions during a news conference at the Arizona Cardinals training facility in Tempe on Feb. 18, 2026. | Mark Henle/The Republic / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Now that Arizona Cardinals training camp has begun, even if this stage is just helmets and shorts, the new offensive system is being explained and explained again to everyone on this year’s roster. A lot of new players can sometimes be a good thing. RELATED: CARSON BECK SIGNS ROOKIE CONTRACT Offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett went through a Q&A session after practice on Saturday. Here is what he had to say. ———————————————————————————————————————— Q: How do you think you’re doing in terms of just getting started here in training camp 3 days in? Hackett: Great. It’s really an extension of OTAs. We don’t have full pads on. That’s when we’re really going to be excited as a group. But just from a mental and operational standpoint, it’s been great for the guys. Just everybody coming back, you always wonder how much is going to stick. And I really feel like they’ve done a nice job. Q: How’s it been having Jacoby (Brissett) back and just what does he bring at quarterback? Hackett: Oh, he’s great. He’s a veteran. He’s been in this league for a long time. I’ve known him for a long time, and it’s great to have him in there, and he’s just working through learning everything, and it’s a nice little process. Q: How different is he from the guy that you saw at the Senior Bowl? Hackett: He’s a lot older. Not as old as me. I was a lot younger back in those days. But you know he’s got that veteran presence. When you first get the rookies, they don’t know what’s going on. So, I think that just the conversations, the things that he’s gone through, just his understanding of football, and the different systems he’s been in. I think all those things help him with us, and you see that growth and just his wisdom. Q: What are some more of the things about his skill set that you think will fit well in your in this offense? Hackett: I think before I go there, it’s one of those things I want him to come into the offense and see what he can do. But just throughout all my experience going against him, he’s a big strong guy that is not afraid to sling it in there. And I think that’s something you’re always excited about. And we’ll see how it goes as we move forward. Q: When you talk about the rookies not knowing what’s going on, exactly what are you talking about? Hackett: Is it like they don’t know their directions around the facility, the playbook, how to just keep their schedule from college to the pros, everything. Everything you can imagine. Coming to this league is just the speed is so different. You talk about the speed being in a new building; a lot of the guys nowadays might be in different rooms and different facilities because of all the transfers and stuff. But most of the time they’ve been in one place for a while, and now it’s a whole new environment. New people, new people to work with, and definitely new playbooks that are very, very intricate due to the fact of all the things that we see and all the different just our defense is out there. You get almost everything and more, which is great because it helps you for the season. But for a young player to have to be able to adjust and learn just the basic system and then apply it to different defenses. It takes some time. So, heads are spinning right now. Especially after two days. But I think it’ll just get better and better. That’s the goal. Q: How do you think Carson (Beck) is dealing with that in two days? Hackett: I’ll tell you, Carson works really hard. I don’t think I even knew from that standpoint how he would be, and I think he’s done a great job learning as much as he possibly can. And he’s really grasping it. But it’s still about getting those reps, which is so critical at this position. And even just with pads is going to be huge because the live situations, the practice pads, no pads, it’s so different. Just on the timing of the routes, how people block, just everything is different. So, it’s just going to keep getting better, but he’s a very hard worker, and I appreciate that from him. Q: How do you assess kind of what he’s shown throughout spring and then these first two practices? Hackett: You assess every single thing, every step, and every movement. I think my favorite thing about him is if you give him a correction, he doesn’t do the same thing twice. He learns from it, and I appreciate that. And he doesn’t let it affect him. So, I think that that’s what you want, and we grow from there. Love his arm strength, love his footwork, intelligence, all those things. He’s done a fine job, and we just got a long way to go. Q: Does having an elite tight end change how a coordinator wants to structure an offense? Hackett: I’ll tell you, he’s fun to be on the same field with. Usually, you have specific things that you do with each position. The more guys that you have that can do more things, the more exciting it is from our standpoint. So, I think to have a guy like Trey (McBride) makes the tight end room really solid. And all those guys. Elijah (Higgins) is doing really well, and he can do more things. So, it allows you to put them in different spots, create different matchups. There are so many different things, and at the same time, they can still run block. We’ll see that as the pads come on, when we finally get to test that. But anytime you have guys that can do multiple things, it’s fun. Our wide receivers, they can run all kinds of different routes instead of just being very specific. So, it just lets you be more fluid. Q: You mentioned Carson’s arm strength. That was one of the questions about him coming out of college, right? You’re pretty pleased with his arm strength so far? Hackett: I am. I am. I don’t know where that came from. I sure enjoy watching him throw the ball down the field. He had a couple really nice ones, and for him tying his feet in and getting the timing of it and then actually calling those things and getting those opportunities. Those are things that we just can’t get enough for him. But up to this point, he’s been able to place the ball all over the field. Q: When you’re mentioning an offense for the first time, what techniques do you use to to teach it? Hackett: I think that’s kind of the magic sauce, you know? It’s the process that you go about. Because the reality of it is, obviously, Coach LaFleur, myself, the coaches, we know it really well. We’ve put it together. We’ve built it. But it doesn’t matter necessarily for us. It’s the guys have to own it. They have to go out there, and it has to be second nature to them. For me, it’s always been about processes. It’s how you break it down one step at a time. Just don’t jump to “Z.” You have to start with everything beforehand and be very, very specific in the things that you want to teach and how you teach them. There might be something you’re very excited to get to, but there are a couple other steps. As long as you can stay organized and understand what you’re trying to accomplish and have a goal each day, I think that’s the best way to do it. A couple of days ago, to do it and especially not trying to get ahead of yourself when you know what’s coming up. These guys have run the pieces before different schemes. Like, is that hard not to get it? Of course. I think you’re always battling that because, especially as a coach, you see something and you’re like, “Oh, let’s do this or let’s game plan this.” And it’s like, “Hold on, let’s think, our foundation right now is let’s get up there. Let’s operate. Let’s be great in those little things first and then be able to build off that.” Even though you can sit there and say, “Oh, well, we could do this versus this or this versus that.” That’s the chess game that we play. But you can’t play chess if you don’t know the basic rules first. So, I think for us right…

title: Former Cardinals TE Vokolek retires after neck scare
summary: A lot of players come and go in the NFL. Usually when they hang up their cleats, it is because their roster options have dried up and their agent’s phone stopped ringing. Not true for Travis Vokolek, a former Arizona Cardinals tight end. He is retiring at the age of 28 due to a serious […]
full_text: GLENDALE, AZ - OCTOBER 05: Travis Vokolek #81 of the Arizona Cardinals runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL football game against the Tennessee Titans at State Farm Stadium on October 5, 2025 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images A lot of players come and go in the NFL. Usually when they hang up their cleats, it is because their roster options have dried up and their agent’s phone stopped ringing. Not true for Travis Vokolek, a former Arizona Cardinals tight end. He is retiring at the age of 28 due to a serious neck injury he suffered last year in Week 6 on the road against the Indianapolis Colts, according to Tyler Drake of ArizonaSports.com . RELATED: TRAINING CAMP TIGHT END OUTLOOK In the play, Vokolek was pushed by Colts linebacker Segun Olubi on a kickoff. Vokolek then landed wrong and hit the ground awkwardly. The stretcher was summoned with both of his arms strapped down, and was taken off the field via the medical cart. He was listed on the depth chart as the TE3 who had duties on special teams mainly. He did have some offensive time in four of the first five games of the 2025 season. He ended the year with 32 offensive snaps and 45 special teams plays. Vololek played for the Cardinals for three seasons. View this post on Instagram Vololek gave a detailed description of his football life on Instagram, and what led to his decision to retire from professional football. He ended up on IR, one of 24 rostered players who found this list their new home, and the Cardinals did not tender him a contract this offseason, making him a free agent. After a decent college career at Nebraska, he was not selected in the 2023 NFL draft and then signed with the Baltimore Ravens. He was a last-day cut, then signed to their practice squad. Later in the season, the Cardinals claimed him off Baltimore’s practice squad after an injury to Geoff Swaim. He made Arizona’s roster in both the 2024 and 2025 seasons.

title: Projecting the Falcons roster heading into training camp
summary: The dead zone is nearly over, as Atlanta Falcons training camp begins on Wednesday, July 29. Things have been mostly quiet since my post-draft roster projection back in May, but a few notable roster moves along with reporting from OTAs and minicamp have adjusted my expectations for the Falcons’ 53-man roster slightly. I also finally […]
full_text: Jun 16, 2026; Atlanta, GA, USA; Atlanta Falcons players interact on the field during Minicamp. Mandatory Credit: Dale Zanine-Imagn Images | Dale Zanine-Imagn Images The dead zone is nearly over, as Atlanta Falcons training camp begins on Wednesday, July 29. Things have been mostly quiet since my post-draft roster projection back in May, but a few notable roster moves along with reporting from OTAs and minicamp have adjusted my expectations for the Falcons’ 53-man roster slightly. I also finally got around to watching all the tape from the Browns 2025 offense—you’re welcome—and that changed a few of my assumptions a bit. There are definitely some notable training camp battles to watch, with a few starting spots up for grabs. The back end of the roster is likely to be very competitive with an entirely new offensive coaching staff and head coach in the building. Headlining all of this is a truly open competition for QB1 between veteran Tua Tagovailoa and 2024 first-rounder Michael Penix Jr, the outcome of which could significantly alter Atlanta’s plans for this season and beyond. Let’s dive right in to my latest thoughts on Atlanta’s 2026 53-man roster. The roster projection is also available in both video and audio format, which you can find embedded below. If you enjoyed the written version, consider giving us a click on these platforms as well. Listen to the audio version of this article using the player below, or find it on your favorite podcast platforms. Italics denote a change from the previous roster projection. OFFENSE – 24 Quarterback – 3 Tua Tagovailoa Michael Penix Jr. Trevor Siemian We’ve received little clarity on the quarterback competition through OTAs and minicamp. The hope is that Michael Penix Jr. is ready to return for the start of training camp, and all signs are pointing to that being the plan. For the time being, I’m moving Tua Tagovailoa into the “presumptive starter” spot, simply by virtue of him being the healthiest option at this stage. This will be the biggest and most prominent battle of training camp. Hopefully it’s an exciting duel between two hungry, young QBs looking to prove themselves—and not utterly depressing a la Desmond Ridder vs Marcus Mariota. There’s an outside shot that Jack Strand, with a very impressive camp, could displace Trevor Siemian. Running Back – 4 Bijan Robinson Brian Robinson Jr. Nate Carter Cash Jones While 90%+ of the carries and snaps will be handled by the duo of Bijan Robinson and Brian Robinson Jr., I do think this team may keep four running backs this season. Atlanta may wind up being one of the most run-heavy teams in the NFL (for good reason), and having a stable of talent to rotate in and develop over the course of the season is wise. I feel like I’m Nate Carter’s only remaining believer, so I’ll stay on that hill until something notable changes. There’s been enough chatter around Cash Jones to take his roster chances seriously, especially given his special teams prowess. Tight End – 3 Kyle Pitts Charlie Woerner Austin Hooper After doing a deep dive into the Browns offense, I feel pretty confident that the Falcons will mostly lean on 12 personnel. As a result, keeping a fourth tight end is largely unnecessary. What’s less certain is who emerges as the TE2 alongside Kyle Pitts: the superior blocker in Woerner, or the more well-rounded Hooper? It may be something that changes week-to-week based on the matchup, but it’ll be fascinating to see what this staff values more. Unlike Zac Robinson’s offense, the TE2 will be expected to catch the ball sometimes . Wide Receiver – 5 Drake London Jahan Dotson Zachariah Branch Olamide Zaccheaus Chris Blair I actually feel pretty solid about this wide receiver group. We all know this is not a group that will be ranked highly among the NFL’s best, but that is partially by design. Drake London is the only one from this group who will be heavily targeted—the rest will be role players and specialists. Jahan Dotson has a real opportunity to carve out at least 3-5 targets a game as the WR2 if he can prove himself worthy of that attention, and he’s got the most well-developed route tree of the bunch. Zachariah Branch is the wild card: his yards-after-catch ability and value as a gadget and screen option could lead to him being a lot more involved than expected, especially if the pass protection struggles. Is this finally the year Chris Blair gets on the roster and gets actual playing time? I sure hope so, because this man has more than earned his shot. It helps that he’s one of the only other legitimate outside receivers on the roster with Casey Washington gone. Offensive Line – 9 LT Jake Matthews LG Matthew Bergeron C Ryan Neuzil RG Chris Lindstrom RT Jawaan Taylor T Wanya Morris T Michael Jerrell G Kyle Hinton C/G Corey Levin There’s no sugar-coating it: right tackle is likely to be a sore spot on this offensive line in 2026. Jawaan Taylor is unquestionably a better pass protector than Elijah Wilkinson, but his run blocking is typically very poor. I’m not sure how Atlanta will work around that issue—perhaps Bill Callahan can work some magic with Taylor? Swing tackle is also a total question mark now with Storm Norton out for the season once again. The Falcons brought in Wanya Morris from the Chiefs, who does have plenty of experience on both sides, but struggled when pressed into action. It’s an acknowledgement that the other options on the roster were not up to the task, so at least the team is being proactive about it. The good news is the other four starting spots are rock solid or better. Jake Matthews remains one of the most consistent left tackles in the NFL, although his ceiling is lower than it once was. Ryan Neuzil once again gets a big vote of confidence from the staff and should continue to grow. Atlanta’s guard tandem could emerge as one of the best in the league, as Matthew Bergeron took a significant step in 2025 and Chris Lindstrom is arguably the best right guard in the NFL. If this line can stay healthy, they should remain very good—even if right tackle is not quite up to par. DEFENSE – 26 Edge Defender – 5 Jalon Walker Samson Ebukam Azeez Ojulari Cameron Thomas Bralen Trice EXEMPT/SUSPENDED: James Pearce Jr. No significant changes here. I do still expect James Pearce Jr. to begin the year with some kind of suspension, but it’s possible the NFL delays discipline until Pearce completes his program. Perhaps if everything goes well, the league just lets it go? Who knows. If Pearce is out of the lineup, the rest of the group will need to pick up the slack. Luckily, Atlanta brought in a number of quality veteran options to improve the rotation. I’m still pulling for Bralen Trice—when he’s been on the field, he’s looked promising. But he must stay healthy through camp or it’s probably the end of the road. The special teams prowess and versatility of DeAngelo Malone or the untapped upside of UFL standout Keshawn Banks could also threaten his spot. Interior Defensive Line – 6 Brandon Dorlus Zach Harrison LaCale London Da’Shawn Hand Maason Smith Anterio Thompson I still really like this interior defensive line and think it could be one of the deepest and best pass rushing units in the league. The run defense is still a big question mark, but the additions of guys of Da’Shawn Hand and maybe Maason Smith should help in that regard. I know many believe another veteran will potentially get a sixth spot here, but I don’t really see the point. That player will be inactive the vast majority of the time. Atlanta drafted Anterio Thompson to develop him, and he’s a good special teams player. I think they’ll try to stash him on the roster as long as possible—though injuries could force their hand and eventually move him to the practice squad. Linebacker – 5 Divine Deablo Christian Harris Kendal Daniels Harold Perkins Jr. Troy Andersen This will be a very different linebacker corps in 2026. The loss of Kaden Elliss is significant, but in some ways he was not a…

full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 15: Anterio Thompson #54 of the Washington Huskies celebrates his sack against the Purdue Boilermakers at Husky Stadium on November 15, 2025 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the Falcons drafted Anterio Thompson, he looked like an upside addition who would likely need some time to crack the team’s rotation on the interior. That’s still true, but injury is delaying his chance to make his case for any playing time at all in 2026. Thompson hasn’t been with the team much or practiced owing to the injury, which we haven’t gotten much in the way of clarity about. What we do know is that he’s now been placed on the non-football injury list by the team, which comes after rookies reported for training camp on Friday. The #Falcons have declared rookie DT Anterio Thompson as having a non-football injury. He will remain on the active list. — Marc Raimondi (@marcraimondi) July 25, 2026 The hope is that Thompson returns soon and gets to make his case for playing time; if he can’t we might be looking at a lost 2026 for the rookie. That would be a shame given that the Falcons clearly saw something they liked in Thompson, who spent 2025 with the Washington Huskies and flashed some promise as a disruptive force on their defensive line. With all-world defensive line coach Nate Ollie overseeing his development, there’s a chance that potential translates into a role as a high-end reserve, but that’s all conjecture until the rookie gets out there and can show what he can do. Atlanta’s defensive front will almost certainly include Zach Harrison, Brandon Dorlus, Maason Smith, Da’Shawn Hand, and LaCale London, with Chris Williams, Ross Blacklock, Carlos Allen Jr., Devonnsha Maxwell, and Thompson competing for a spot or two and practice squad slots. The sooner Thompson can get back out there, the better, so we’ll hope it’s very soon.

title: Falcons make massive moves in early 2026 predictions
summary: Welcome to the start of football season. Training camp is just getting underway, and the football landscape is littered with ambition and golden promises. Every question mark is answered with the best-case scenario; every breakout player will be the most actualized version of themselves come this time next season. That’s why when bold predictors like […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA OCTOBER 08: Houston quarterback C.J. Stroud (7) rolls out of the pocket during the NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Atlanta Falcons on October 8th, 2023 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to the start of football season. Training camp is just getting underway, and the football landscape is littered with ambition and golden promises. Every question mark is answered with the best-case scenario; every breakout player will be the most actualized version of themselves come this time next season. That’s why when bold predictors like SB Nation’s Jarrett Bailey go out on a limb to predict 61 different aspects of the 2026 season, I have no choice but to respect the game. To put yourself out there and plant your flag this early on topics like “Who’s going to win the Super Bowl?” or even something as trivial as “Who’s throwing the most passing touchdowns this season?” is a level of courage that I haven’t acquired yet. So, is it possible that none of these things will happen? Absolutely. Maybe it’s even likely. But it is a cool way to dive into the minds of some of these guys who also wake up and think about this beautiful game 24/7/365. So, let’s dive into these predictions, and more importantly, what Bailey said about the Atlanta Falcons. 1) Bijan Robinson ranks third in rushing yards, falls out of top five (again) in rushing TDs After discussing 29 other topics that don’t necessarily affect the Falcons, Bailey lists out his top five league leaders in 10 different categories, including rushing yards and rushing touchdowns. In rushing yards, Robinson slots in at third with 1,427 yards, behind only James Cook (1,493) and Jahmyr Gibbs (1,648). This could be a sore spot for Falcons fans, as the battle of “which running back is more valuable” continues to rage on even into this season, as both are up for extensions and neither is willing to blink first to get the lesser amount of the two backs. That being said, neither of the two 2023 first-round picks shows up on the rushing touchdowns list as new Kansas City Chief Kenneth Walker takes the crown with 15 scores. The Broncos’ Javonte Williams and Ravens’ Derrick Henry tied for fourth with 12. 2) Drake London is not a top-five producer in receptions, receiving yards nor receiving touchdowns I think this is more a statement on how poor the Falcons quarterback situation may get in 2026; more on that to come, but the newly minted number-one receiver for Atlanta didn’t breach the top five in receptions. Cincinnati Bengals’ Ja’Marr Chase snatches the triple crown in this exercise, leading in receptions (128), yards (1,693) and touchdowns (20). A wild prediction since we’ve never had a receiver hit 125+ receptions, 1600 receiving yards and 20 touchdowns. The closest we’ve gotten is our latest triple-crown recipients: Chase in 2024 (127, 1708, 17), Cooper Kupp in 2021 (145, 1947, 16) and the G.O.A.T. Jerry Rice in 1995 (122, 1848, 15). All this could mean is that London is right there, sitting around 100 receptions and 1200 yards again, as he did in 2024, especially with the more run-heavy approach we expect Kevin Stefanski to deploy. Or, we could be looking at another year of wasted Drake London, Kyle Pitts, and Bijan Robinson routes as the search for a franchise quarterback continues. But we’re not getting into that yet; first, we have a terrible prediction to divulge. 3) The Aints win the NFC South Listen, call it what you want: Hype around the unknown that is Tyler Shough, the buzz around their young head coach, Kellen Moore, the way that New Orleans’ defense had the fourth-best defense in EPA/play after their Week 12 bye last season. Still, the hype machine surrounding that team in the bayou has been loud, and only getting louder. “Another team I’m very bullish on is the New Orleans Saints. The additions they’ve made this offseason should have their fans excited. Jordyn Tyson taken in the first round to complement Chris Olave, Travis Etienne coming off the best season of his career and now being paired with Alvin Kamara, David Edwards at guard, cornerback Martin Emerson on a cheap deal. This is a team that won four of its last five games in 2025, and Tyler Shough showed real progress in that stretch – they win a wide open division and host a playoff game for the first time since 2020.” It sickens me that they may be getting better as the Falcons potentially bottom out in an attempt to find themselves in the NFL landscape. But it has been amazing watching them take their medicine after they continuously tried to beat the salary cap, and hopefully that will continue. In this scenario, the Falcons will be bitter about missing the opportunity to stomp on the Saints more while they’re down, but that’s all about to change with the fourth and final bit of this exercise for the Falcons…and it’s a doozy. 4) Falcons trade for CJ Stroud “The Falcons have a really nice collection of talent on offense, with Bijan Robinson being who many believe is the top running back in the NFL, and Drake London is one of the game’s finest receivers. Unfortunately, they have yet to find a quarterback who they can lean on, and that will continue to be the case in 2026 with Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix. Atlanta trades for Stroud, who easily becomes the best quarterback Kevin Stefanski has had since Baker Mayfield…” Immediately, what comes to mind is what it would cost to obtain a 26-year-old quarterback who was the clear Offensive Rookie of the Year in 2023. If the Texans believe that they can find a better solution to the position in the draft, especially with the window currently afforded by their impressive defense, there is a chance they could move on from Stroud, but what would the cost be? For the Texans to fall short of their goals, probably an AFC Championship game appearance, it would more than likely fall on Stroud not being up to the task for the second year in a row. The price for a quarterback that has shown the flashes that Stroud has at 26 probably begins with three first-round draft picks, even with his recent struggles. I can’t see Ian Cunningham getting rid of that kind of capital, even if Stroud would be an intriguing addition.

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: defensive tackle T.J. Sanders
summary: The Buffalo Bills aren’t known for playing their defensive linemen in multiple positions like they are their offensive linemen. Usually, if a player is drafted as a defensive end, that’s where he’s playing. The same goes for defensive tackle, although there is some nuance to that given the former defense’s need for one-tech and three-tech […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NY - SEPTEMBER 18: T.J. Sanders #98 of the Buffalo Bills lines up before the snap during an NFL football game against the Miami Dolphins at Highmark Stadium on September 18, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills aren’t known for playing their defensive linemen in multiple positions like they are their offensive linemen. Usually, if a player is drafted as a defensive end, that’s where he’s playing. The same goes for defensive tackle, although there is some nuance to that given the former defense’s need for one-tech and three-tech players. Sometimes, though, there are players who can fill multiple roles up front. Rare are the players who can go both inside and outside along the defensive line, but last year, the Bills ended up playing a rookie in a more versatile role. Was that sheerly out of necessity, or were the Bills forecasting that player’s future? Perhaps it’s a self-fulfilling prophecy, but in today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss a young player who will likely see time at multiple spots along Buffalo’s new-look defensive line. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: T.J. Sanders Number: 98 Position: DT Height/Weight: 6’4” 297 lbs. Age: 23 (24 on 7/30/2027) Experience/Draft: 2; selected by Buffalo in the second round (No. 41 overall) of the 2025 NFL Draft) College: South Carolina Acquired: Second-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Sanders enters the second year of his four-year rookie contract. For the 2026 seaosn, his cap hit is $2,419,411. If he’s released, Buffalo will carry a dead cap charge of $8,136,967. 2025 Recap: In the early going, Sanders played more than perhaps Buffalo thought he would thanks to an injury to Ed Oliver. Sanders was pushed around in those early matchups, as he was consistently beaten at the point of attack, and he looked especially weak in his anchor against the run. He totaled just two tackles in his first four games. However, a knee injury suffered before Buffalo played the New England Patriots led the team to place him on injured reserve. When he returned, he looked like a far better player. Sanders was activated from IR ahead of Buffalo’s Week Eleven matchup with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and he had three tackles in that game alone. He finished the regular season strong, and he even made his first career starts in Buffalo’s last two regular season games. He played a mix of defensive tackle and defensive end, proving to be quite versatile in addition to showing his overall improvement. He had 16 tackles, one sack, and one pass knockdown during the regular season. Although he played 35 total snaps in the playoffs, he did not register on the stat sheet. Positional outlook: Sanders is one of eight defensive tackles listed on the current roster. Tommy Akingbesote, DeWayne Carter, Deone Walker, Ed Oliver, Zion Logue, Zane Durant, and Phidarian Mathis are the others. Landon Jackson and Kody Huisman are listed at defensive end, which is another spot where Sanders may see time this season. 2026 Offseason: Sanders is healthy and participating in offseason work to date. 2026 Season outlook: As strange as it seems, Sanders’ experience at multiple spots last season will likely give him a leg up this year in new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s scheme. It wasn’t exactly ideal to watch Sanders, who we assumed would be a three-tech defensive tackle in former head coach Sean McDermott’s scheme, play defensive end, but in Leonhard’s new odd-man front, it’s not only possible that Sanders will line up at DE, it’s likely. Arguably, Sanders played better at defensive end last season than he did at defensive tackle, so perhaps McDermott was on to something when he was playing Sanders there out of necessity. Sanders is a roster lock this season, but his role is what we’ll have to see as the Bills move through camp. Ideally, he sees significant time as a starting down lineman in a 4i or 5-tech role. He’ll need to be better in his anchor, and hopefully a year in a professional strength and conditioning program will help in that regard. Can Sanders find the gear that he showed while a member of the Gamecocks, where he totaled 17.5 tackles for loss and 9.5 sacks across three seasons? That would certainly be nice, but Buffalo can’t necessarily count on that, either. We don’t know how often Leonhard will rotate his defensive linemen, so it’s possible that Sanders could be in line for a greater percentage of snaps than he had under McDermott, who was notorious for rotating his defensive line constantly within games. Either way, the Bills would like to see Sanders take a great leap forward in his second season. Shifting to a more attack-oriented defense could be just what the doctor ordered, and Sanders has the ability to play multiple spots on the defensive line. He’ll be a big part of the rotation this year provided that he stays healthy.

title: Dalton Kincaid is a TE2 according to ESPN fantasy experts
summary: Now that we are just days away from the start of training camp for the Buffalo Bills, it is time to review the fantasy expectations for our final positional group. As one might expect, the depth of the tight ends on the roster have likely diminished fantasy expectations for this season. The highest ranked option […]
full_text: SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 2: Dalton Kincaid #86 of the Buffalo Bills participates during a Pro Bowl team practice during the NFL Pro Bowl Games at Moscone Center South on February 2, 2026 in San Francisco, California. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images Now that we are just days away from the start of training camp for the Buffalo Bills, it is time to review the fantasy expectations for our final positional group. As one might expect, the depth of the tight ends on the roster have likely diminished fantasy expectations for this season. The highest ranked option is still Dalton Kincaid, as the former first round pick has flashed his potential when healthy. The collective rankings according to ESPN have Kincaid ranked as the 15th best tight end, just behind Mark Andrews (Baltimore Ravens) and Isaiah Likely (New York Giants). Kincaid would likely be ranked higher if healthy, with his 37% snap share in 2025 noted as a reason for any skepticism. With that being said, the statistical projections show an increase for Kincaid in 2026 with 698 receiving yards on 59 receptions. Dawson Knox does not crack the top 25 rankings on ESPN, and he is projected to have a statistical dip this season. This can be accounted to the uptick in production for Kincaid, as Knox is projected to finish with 25 receptions for 265 yards. While Knox remains a valuable piece of the Bills offense, at this point he is likely a bye week waiver wire addition. The expectations for second-year tight end Jackson Hawes also remain in check – with a projection of 11 receptions for 110 yards. Hawes may see more playing time this season, but his value comes from his work as a blocking tight end. Are you more optimistic about Kincaid’s chances this season? If not, do you see Knox as a roster-worthy addition? Be sure to share your thoughts in the comments section below.

Age: 26 (27 on 9/22/2026) Experience/Draft: 6; selected by the Los Angeles Chargers in the third round (No. 77 overall) of the 2021 NFL Draft College: Tennessee Acquired: Signed with Buffalo on 3/13/2025 Financial situation (per Spotrac): Palmer enters the second year of his three-year, $36 million contract. If he’s on the 53-man roster, he carries a cap hit of $11.75 million, which is the fifth-highest total on Buffalo’s roster. If he’s released, Buffalo will carry a dead cap charge of $14.24 million for the season. If he’s traded, Buffalo will carry a $1.6 million dead cap hit this year and a $4.8 million dead cap hit in 2027. Asa vested veteran, Palmer’s $9.66 million base salary becomes fully guaranteed if he’s on the roster Week One. 2025 Recap: Palmer came over from the Chargers last season, and he was immediately expected to slot in as either the second or third wideout in Buffalo’s passing attack, with Khalil Shakir the clear top receiver. Instead, Palmer was a nonfactor for much of the season. The initial returns were solid, as he caught five passes for 61 yards on nine targets in Buffalo’s season-opening 41-40 victory over the Baltimore Ravens. That was the high-water mark, however, as he did not catch more than two passes in a game for the rest of the season. In the first quarter of Buffalo’s Week Six tilt against the Atlanta Falcons, it looked like Palmer might have a coming-out party, as he caught two passes for 60 yards. However, he injured his knee and his ankle on the same play, which caused him to miss the next three games. When he returned, he was still limited by the injuries, and he missed two more games as a result. Faced with roster decisions and mounting injuries at the receiver position, Buffalo placed Palmer on injured reserve ahead of the postseason, ending his season before he could appear in a playoff game. He finished his disappointing campaign with just 22 receptions for 303 yards on 37 targets. All of those totals were career-lows. Positional outlook: Palmer is one of 14 wideouts on the current roster. Khalil Shakir, Keon Coleman, DJ Moore, Skyler Bell, Mac Dalena, Mecole Hardman Jr., Ja’Mori Maclin, Jalen Virgil, Trent Sherfield, Tyrell Shaver, Stephen Gosnell, Max Tomczak, and Quentin Skinner are the others. 2026 Offseason: Palmer was still rehabbing his injuries at the start of offseason work, but he was a full participant during minicamp. He is healthy now. He did not have surgery to repair his injuries, choosing rest and rehabilitation over surgery. 2026 Season outlook: It’s easy to say that injuries caused Palmer’s season to be a dud last year, but that’s an oversimplification. He was a nonfactor for much of the year even before he was hurt, and while we can debate whether the Bills mismanaged his injuries by not putting him on injured reserve after that Monday Night Football loss to the Falcons, what we do know is that he was not terribly useful for Buffalo’s offense. Add in the fact that his cap hit is the fifth-highest on the team, and we have all the makings of an abysmal contract. Nothing about Palmer’s play—not his time in college with Tennessee or his performance with the Chargers—suggested that he should be paid like a top-50 wideout in the NFL, but his contract has him at WR42 right now. That’s a pretty huge miss on the part of general manager Brandon Beane. One good thing to come from that contract was Beane realizing that he needed to add receiving help this offseason, so the Bills went out and traded for a legitimate stud in DJ Moore. We can argue about whether that was an overpay another time. Palmer is likely to be on the Bills’ roster this season. I don’t think they’ll eat the huge dead cap hit by releasing him, and I’d be very surprised if they found a trade partner given Palmer’s horrendous 2025 showing. Allocating top-five cap dollars to someone who’s probably fighting, at best, to be WR3 isn’t ideal, but it’s legitty for the Bills this season. Hopefully, Palmer can bounce back and be a meaningful contributor to a revamped Bills’ passing offense. However, I wouldn’t be surprised if he’s used in a far more niche role this season, especially if Coleman and Bell can beat him out for snaps. Palmer averaged 46 catches, 572 receiving yards, and 3 touchdowns per year with the Chargers. If he can approach those numbers this season, it will be a win for the Bills. I’m not a gambler, but I’d bet the under on all three of those totals, though. Palmer is not someone I’m counting on as a big contributor this season, though I wouldn’t mind being proven wrong.

summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - DECEMBER 11: Carolina Panthers guard Andrew Norwell (68) during the game between the Carolina Panthers and the San Diego Chargers on December 11, 2016 at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, NC. Panthers win 28-16 over the Chargers. (Photo by Jim Dedmon/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #49. Andrew Norwell Everyone loves a story about an undrafted free agent becoming a high level NFL player. Andrew Norwell is an interesting, and perhaps the least surprising version of that story. Norwell was a highly regarded recruit coming out of high school, ranked as either a four start or five star prospect, depending on where you look. He went to Ohio State, where he developed into a two time All Big Ten honoree. Despite the prestigious pedigree and decorated college career, Norwell somehow went undrafted in the 2014 NFL Draft. The Panthers were fortunate enough to scoop enough, and boy did that work out for them. He was forced into the starting lineup in Week 7 of his rookie year and would never relinquish that spot. He finished out the season as arguably the best rookie lineman and one of the best interior lineman in the whole league. He would go on to be a staple of the Panthers offensive line for the next three seasons and would perform as one of the league’s best guards, though he didn’t get a lot of recognition for it. He finally got his flowers after the 2017 season, when he was named first team all pro. The Jaguars would lure him away from Carolina with the largest contract for a guard in the entire NFL. Norwell would finish out his career with four seasons in Jacksonville and one last rodeo for Ron Rivera in Washington in 2022. Norwell was an interesting case of a highly regarded player throughout his amateur case that didn’t get drafted and then went on to become a very good NFL player. It’s like the least surprising success story for an undrafted free agent of all time. But credit to the Panthers for getting him to come here and giving him an opportunity to shine. Norwell only spent four seasons in Carolina, but he was one of the best players in the league at his position during those four years. His time coincided with what were some pretty good offensive seasons by the Rivera era Panthers standards, and he was a big part of that. He was part of the team that made it to Super Bowl 50 and the groups that went to the playoffs in 2014 and 2017. His rise from undrafted free agent and the elite player he was during a high point in Panthers history earns him spot number 49 on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

title: Chicago Bears 2026 Training Camp Position Breakdown: Quarterback
summary: There’s zero drama in the Chicago Bears quarterback room this season, which is exactly what we want. Last year, head coach Ben Johnson showed us how he wants his QB room to shape up, and with all three players back, it’ll be business as usual. Roster Locks Caleb Williams is on the cusp of something […]
full_text: SAN DIEGO, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 27: Caleb Williams #13 congratulates Miller Moss #7 of the USC Trojans after defeating the Louisville Cardinals 42-28 in the DIRECTV Holiday Bowl at Petco Park on December 27, 2023 in San Diego, California. (Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images) | Getty Images There’s zero drama in the Chicago Bears quarterback room this season, which is exactly what we want. Last year, head coach Ben Johnson showed us how he wants his QB room to shape up, and with all three players back, it’ll be business as usual. Roster Locks Caleb Williams is on the cusp of something special. Most of our fans feel it. Fans of the Vikings, Lions, and especially the Packers feel it, which is why they spend so much time online talking about him. The NFL feels it, which is why he’s been one of their most marketed players. And his peers feel it, which is why he was voted number 51 of the Top 100 Players list. He was so good in 2025, while still having so much more room to grow. And that’s not lost on him. “There’s so much to unlock,” he said via the team site, “there’s so much to get better at, there’s so much left of ball for me and us and accolades that we’ll have as a team.” He’s paired with a like-minded head coach in Ben Johnson, and their parallel drive for greatness is exactly what you want from the QB/head coach relationship. His backup is Tyson Bagent, and I’m so glad the silliness around him has died down, because he’s a good football player. He hasn’t taken a meaningful rep since his rookie year, but the quality tape he put together during each preseason, plus the coaching he’s received from Ben and the Bears’ offensive staff, could land him an even bigger payday (he inked a 2-year, $10 million deal last year) when he’s a free agent in 2028. Johnson bringing in Case Keenum to be a veteran presence in the room paid dividends. In January, during the week the Bears were preparing to play the Los Angeles Rams in the divisional round of the playoffs, Ben spoke about what Keenum meant to their 2026 season. From Nicholas Moreano’s social media . “He’s been an integral part of what we’ve done. He’s been tremendous in terms of Caleb’s growth. That was really the thought process of bringing him in, a guy with skins on the wall. He’s played in big games himself at a high level. He’s won big games. He’s lost big games. His experience has been something that all these young players can really lean into, particularly in weeks like this, where you come off an emotional win and yet you’ve got to turn your sights onto the next page pretty quickly. The vision we had bringing him in, it’s been pretty incredible. I give Ryan (Poles) a lot of credit for that. As we’re talking about, in the springtime, how do we best help our young quarterback grow and develop? Case’s name came up pretty quickly in that process, and it’s just been a phenomenal fit. I know if he ever needed to play, I know he could still play at a high level too. We see that every day at practice as well.” This is a strong quarterback room, and one analyst recently ranked Chicago’s backup situation the sixth-best in the NFL. “While he’s seen minimal work over the last couple of seasons, Bagent was solid in a four-game stretch as the starter in 2023,” wrote CBS Sports’ Tyler Sullivan a couple of days ago. “He led Chicago to a 2-2 record while completing 65.1% of his passes, totaling four touchdowns (three passing and one rushing) and five interceptions. Along with Bagent, the Bears have Case Keenum, who has over a decade of league experience, including 66 regular-season starts. His best season game in 2017 when he went 11-3 as the starter for Minnesota in the regular season and helped them advance to the NFC Championship after the Minneapolis Miracle. His most recent starts came back over two weeks in 2023 as a member of the Texans. He completed 64.2% of his passes, but had just one passing touchdown to three interceptions. While Bagent would be the first man up after Williams, having Keenum as a third option isn’t too shabby, given his experience. A Good Bet To Make It See above… Roster Bubble/Practice Squad If the Bears carry three on the active roster, that leaves little room for a fourth on the practice squad. However, with Keenum being 38 years old, maybe UDFA Miller Moss catches Ben Johnson’s eye, and they decide his upside is worth sticking around. “His tape popped off,” Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor said about Moss via FOX32 . “This is a player that can play on time, that can be an accurate passer, that can win from the pocket, and has enough ability to move around when need be. You just saw a poise. You see an experienced guy that played a lot of football. The way he operates in the huddle, the way he operates in the meeting room, it is all stuff that we heard from the coaches that have worked with him in the past in college.” Regardless of what happens in Chicago, Moss, who was Caleb’s backup at USC for two years, will do his best to put some good tape together during the preseason. Give us your thoughts on the Bears’ QB room?

title: Bears have two of the top 32 Tight Ends in the NFL
summary: In 2025, the Chicago Bears used 12 personnel (one running back, two tight ends), the sixth-most in the league, and 13 personnel, the fifth-most. Overall, the Bears played with at least two tight ends on the field about 45% of the time. So those numbers are high, but how did the offense perform in those […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - SEPTEMBER 08: Colston Loveland #84 of the Chicago Bears and Cole Kmet #85 of the Chicago Bears during the second half against the Minnesota Vikings on September 8, 2025 at Solider Field in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Melissa Tamez/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images In 2025, the Chicago Bears used 12 personnel (one running back, two tight ends), the sixth-most in the league, and 13 personnel, the fifth-most. Overall, the Bears played with at least two tight ends on the field about 45% of the time. So those numbers are high, but how did the offense perform in those situations? In EPA (Expected Points Added), the Bears were eighth best when in 12 personnel and ninth best when in 13, so it makes sense that this will continue to be a big part of Ben Johnson’s offense. Pro Football Focus recently ranked the top 32 tight ends in the NFL, and the Bears had two of them. Second-year pro Colston Loveland, who turned 22 in April, ranked fifth, and grizzled veteran Cole Kmet, who is just 27 years old, ranked 31st. “After a quiet start to his rookie campaign, Loveland really turned it on in the second half of the season,” PFF wrote. “The No. 10 overall pick’s 84.0 PFF grade was third among all tight ends in the NFL, while his 1.97 yards per route run were fifth. Loveland’s 597 receiving yards from Week 9 on were second in the league, while his 193 yards in the playoffs led all tight ends despite the Bears losing in the divisional round.” Loveland’s talent and versatility give him a legitimate chance at being the best tight end in the NFL in 2026. “Kmet continues to play an important role despite the presence of star youngster Colston Loveland,” PFF continued. “While Kmet hasn’t quite recaptured his peak receiving performance, he’s still averaged over 10 yards per reception in each of the past two seasons while tallying six touchdowns in the process. Kmet’s value as a blocker is also extremely important when it comes to maintaining the flexibility in Ben Johnson’s offense.” These two are a big reason why, in our latest Reacts poll, you voted the Bears’ tight end position group as the one you’re most confident in. But it’s not the only reason, because the Bears spent a second-round draft pick on Stanford’s Sam Roush. Roush brings the reputation of being an exceptional blocker, and that’s exactly what you want in your TE3, but defenses better not underestimate his athleticism. Last month, Bears quarterback Caleb Williams was on the New Heights podcast with Jason and Travis Kelce, and when Travis mentioned that the Bears’ tight end room was one of his favorites in the NFL because “you got two absolute dogs,” Williams was quick to point out Roush. “I got a third one now,” Caleb said. “We got a new guy, new rookie guy. He’s built like the other guys also, tall, smooth, he’s a freak of nature. Run block, pass block, catch, all of that. Whatever we need. We’ve got three of those now. We’re juiced, I’m juiced. It’s always an advantage when you can have one tight end, but when you have three that can do it all, it’s a big advantage.” If the Bears increase their 12 nd 13 use in 2026, then Roush, who will turn 23 in September, will likely get more offensive snaps than last year’s number three tight end, Durham Smythe, who played about a quarter of the time (293 snaps). Roush also brings plenty of experience playing special teams with him (over 500 snaps at Stanford), so he’ll be a factor in the third phase too. Our Partners at FanDuel Sportsbook have Roush with some extremely long odds to win Rookie of the Year (+25,000), but you can get Loveland at -114 to go over or under 775.5 receiving yards. If you’re feeling really lucky, you can grab Loveland to win Offensive Player of the Year at +10,000. title: WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football: Assessing Brandon Robinson’s Roster
summary: Well, we’ve done it. With this assessment, we’ve looked at all 14 rosters in the WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football League and examined all of them for strengths, weaknesses, and where they could improve. Our last roster in this series is the roster of Brandon Robinson. Brandon has had a solid roster that has been competing […]
full_text: Woodland Hills, - June 08:Rams Myles Garrett (95) at Rams practice on Monday, June 8, 2026. (Photo by David Crane/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images Well, we’ve done it. With this assessment, we’ve looked at all 14 rosters in the WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football League and examined all of them for strengths, weaknesses, and where they could improve. Our last roster in this series is the roster of Brandon Robinson. Brandon has had a solid roster that has been competing for titles the last couple of seasons. He hasn’t gotten over the hump. Can this be the year? Let’s take a look. Here’s the roster: I know Brandon has struggled to find a consistent QB1 that he can start. Did he finally find it with Sam Darnold? I’m all for handcuffing QBs, but usually I like to have the starter as well. After Darnold, Brandon has an additional 5 QBs on the roster, and 4 of them are backups, and the other is Tua. There’s not much here after Darnold. In the RB room, Williams and Walker are a nice duo that will start most weeks as long as they are healthy. Having both Jones and Mason does really well to have that room handcuffed as a third option. The WR room looks like it might be in a bit of a transitional phase. Brown and Diggs have been a nice duo at the top of any fantasy team. And with guys like Ridley, Addison, and Pittman behind them, it’s certainly a room that you wouldn’t complain about. Will Brown get back to his big dog status in New England? What will Diggs be this year? Can you get anything out of Ridley? Will Pittman be better or worse in Pittsburgh? There are a lot of questions here. This room can’t be bad, but it may not be as strong as it was a couple of seasons ago. The tight end room has Tre McBride, so it’s automatically a great room. Njoku probably isn’t much of a point-getter anymore, and he’s also 31. This roster could really use something behind McBride. This DT room, when Chris Jones was cleaning up, was strong, but Jones is on his last legs and isn’t the fantasy scorer he used to be. Redmond had a pretty big season last year; can he repeat that performance? He’s a UDFA who keeps getting better; it’ll be interesting to see what he is this year. Will Fiske eat more this year with Garrett in town? What if Donald comes back? What does that do to him? Wyatt is a guy who is probably a bigger name than a fantasy star. This edge room, if TJ Watt is back, paired with Myles Garrett, is just silly good. The guys behind those two are decent rotational guys and can start in a pinch, but Brandon really needs his dynamic duo to stay healthy. The linebacker room is loaded with big names, but it has point getters. A lot of these guys are the types of players that don’t make splashy plays; they just make tackles. That’s not going to do a ton to pivot a game on the field, but it can pivot a fantasy game. Some of these guys may lose snaps this year, but there are plenty of scenarios where finding 3-4 starters in this group won’t be a problem. Brandon hasn’t committed much to the CB room. A strategy I support. The safety room also looks like it has enough point scorers to make some noise. Again, not a ton of high-profile guys, but last year 24 safeties scored 190 or more points in our scoring system, and Brandon had 4 of them. You certainly can’t complain with those results. This is a really solid team. It should put together a really strong starting lineup and has enough depth behind it to pilot any injury storms. There’s no reason this roster shouldn’t be competing for a title this season.
author: Bill Zimmerman

title: WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football: Assessing Tyler Volz’s Roster
summary: Today is our last day of assessing rosters in the WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football League. We have two more rosters to go, so let’s dive into it. Today we look at Tyler Volz. Tyler has been on this team for the jump, and it was largely a middling team until recently. The team has shown […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears celebrates during the first quarter of an NFL divisional playoff game against the Los Angeles Rams at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Today is our last day of assessing rosters in the WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football League. We have two more rosters to go, so let’s dive into it. Today we look at Tyler Volz. Tyler has been on this team for the jump, and it was largely a middling team until recently. The team has shown improvement, become a playoff team, and last season was competing for a title despite coming up short. Here’s the roster: The QB room is great. Two QB1s. I would hate to rely on Bo Nix as my QB1, but as my QB2? Sign me up. Herbert and Nix are a great duo. I’d love a 3rd QB in the room, but tough to complain. Barkley and Brown are a great startable duo. Monangai is a nice rotational guy behind those two, and Stevenson works in that role as well, even if Henderson starts getting more of the load. Tracy is an interesting guy on the roster with the wild card that is Skattebo. The WR room is also loaded. If Justin Jefferson rebounds? With ARSB and Smith (especially with no AJ Brown), that trio could be elite. Williams is a really strong 4th WR; I just don’t love the depth behind the top-end guys. That’s the biggest weakness here, but the starters are elite. The tight end room is another one of those rooms where it’s functional but not spectacular. This room won’t win you any fantasy games, but it probably won’t be the reason you lost either. On the defensive side of the ball is where we start to see some issues. The DT room is fine. It has plenty of functional players; again, they aren’t going to lose you games, but are any of these guys going to go out and drop 20 points in a single game? Not very often. I love that the edge room has Will Anderson at the top. There are also some developmental guys in the mix like Mykel Williams; the rest of the room is loaded with solid guys. Hendrickson is a bigger name than a fantasy star because he doesn’t play the run well. You need tackles, not just sacks. Again, a room of solid guys is nice, but it could use another difference maker to go with Anderson. The LB room looks a lot like the DT room. The room is fine, but it doesn’t have a guy capable of scoring 20 PPG, and you really need one or two of those guys in your LB room to make an elite defense. There are too many CBs. Keep DeJean, cut everyone else. You’re welcome. I’d like to see a few more bodies in the safety room, but the three that are on the roster are all solid guys. Bates and Cross could potentially be a really strong duo. This team is a similar build to the team of Redacted. It has a really strong offense, and the defense isn’t bad; it just doesn’t stand out. When you start more defensive players than offensive players, as we do in this league, a great defense can actually win championships. Tyler is a team that’s contending this year for sure, and the roster is strong enough to win a title, but it needs some players on defense to step up and show that the defense can keep up with the offense. If it can, this team has a shot.
