title: The Rams defensive line shouldn’t need Aaron Donald to be elite
summary: In what has been an exceptionally newsworthy offseason for the Los Angeles Rams, the specter of an Aaron Donald return to the royal and sol is the biggest story of the year. Granted, part of that is influenced by the fact that this is the dead period for NFL news, so our minds cling on […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - JANUARY 14: Aaron Donald #99 of the Los Angeles Rams looks on from the sideline prior to an NFC Wild Card Playoff football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on January 14, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Ryan Kang/Getty Images) | Getty Images In what has been an exceptionally newsworthy offseason for the Los Angeles Rams, the specter of an Aaron Donald return to the royal and sol is the biggest story of the year. Granted, part of that is influenced by the fact that this is the dead period for NFL news, so our minds cling on to the few stories that do exist and turn them into headline news consistently since there’s nothing else going on in the football world until the whole league reports for training camp. But in a spring and summer that has featured a trade for an All-Pro cornerback, a trade for the reigning defensive player of the year and drafting Matthew Stafford’s expected successor in the first round, Donald and his will-he, won’t-he saga still has a chokehold on the league. If he returns to the Rams, it takes the best roster in the league to yet another level. After all, he is one of the best defensive players in NFL history and he’s still young enough that you’re not worried about his body breaking down like you would be when someone like Philip Rivers reemerged from retirement for the end of the 2025 season in Indianapolis. It would be a major boon for that Rams defense. Former Rams DT Aaron Donald is going through a "very strict, regimented process" to decide whether he wants to unretire this season, Rams head coach Sean McVay said. And if Donald does decide he wants to play, McVay said, "we are going to try to be able to make that happen."… — NFL on ESPN (@ESPNNFL) July 25, 2026 They shouldn’t need him to be one of the best defensive fronts in football, however. In fact, the expectation should be that this is one of the most fearsome units in the sport whether Donald suits up or not. Take a look at the talent across the Rams’ front seven. There aren’t many teams in the NFL that have even remotely as much talent and production as this group does. Myles Garrett is currently the best defensive player in the league, at least among front-seven players, and we’ve spent tons of time this offseason discussing how much he’ll help Byron Young (and how high of a floor Young already has). On the line, you start with Kobie Turner, easily one of the best players in the game without a Pro Bowl honor over the last three years. Braden Fiske is healthy and almost certainly hasn’t hit his ceiling yet. And anchoring the middle is the perennially underrated Poona Ford, who’s as good of a run stopper at nose tackle as there is in professional football. Just based on names and reputations alone, that’s a fantastic group. The production backs up the reputations, too. Last season, the Rams ranked fifth in the NFL in pressure rate (per NFL Pro/Next Gen Stats) and eighth in Pass Rush Win Rate (per ESPN). They did that despite ranking 24 th in average get-off time, defined as the average amount of time it takes to get over the line of scrimmage. Who finished first? The Cleveland Browns, led by the Who finished first among qualified defensive linemen in average get-off? Myles Garrett. #49ers GM John Lynch says he shared a John Wooden quote with Kyle Shanahan this offseason: “Don’t lose sleep worrying about your competition. Let them lose sleep worrying about you.” Then the #Rams traded for Myles Garrett… Shanahan’s reaction: “F*** John Wooden.” 😂 pic.twitter.com/DvMWungUrw — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) July 26, 2026 This wasn’t an elite run defense last year by any means, but was solidly middle of the pack in several different statistical categories. Jared Verse, who was shipped off to Cleveland in the Garrett trade, brought a lot to the table as a run stopper off the edge, but it’s not like Garrett is a DPR (designated pass rusher), he’s going to hold up there just fine. The personnel transformation on defense for Los Angeles this offseason has put this franchise in a great position to win it all. The talent is there. The don’t need Aaron Donald back to be the favorites to win the Super Bowl, they already are without him on the roster. It would be remarkable and a no-doubt boost if he returns, but the Rams have done spectacularly well at putting themselves in a position where they don’t need to add another Hall of Famer to spark a championship run. That’s a pretty comfortable spot to be in.
author: Brendan Dzwierzynski

title: PFF QB Annual: Can Matthew Stafford replicate MVP season?
summary: Pro Football Focus (PFF) released its 2026 QB Annual. It’s a deep dive into all things analytics surrounding quarterback performance last season and over their careers. There were some important takeaways for Matthew Stafford in terms of changes that elevated his game en route to the MVP award in 2025. The question moving forward is […]
full_text: SEATTLE, CA - JANUARY 25: Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford (9) looks to the sidelines during warm ups before the NFC championship game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on Sunday, Jan. 25, 2026 in Seattle, CA. (Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images) Pro Football Focus (PFF) released its 2026 QB Annual . It’s a deep dive into all things analytics surrounding quarterback performance last season and over their careers. There were some important takeaways for Matthew Stafford in terms of changes that elevated his game en route to the MVP award in 2025. The question moving forward is which pieces are sustainable and which may be primed for regression. Let’s dive into the annual and put its predictive powers to good use. A new scheme wrinkle With the Rams deploying heavier personnel and addition tight ends more often last season, Stafford moved from a heavily shotgun quarterback to playing under center more often than anyone. In some ways this is a scheme change that sent the NFL back to the early 2000’s. It is truly the best way to marry the run and pass games, and we often saw tight ends and receivers disguised as blockers only to leak out into routes. It’s the latest and most impressive wrinkle from Sean McVay and it worked to great effect for Stafford. Stafford was the quarterback most often under center on a percentage basis and the least often in the shotgun according to PFF: And the Rams went to this well often because it worked. Stafford’s PFF passing grade was better under center than in the shotgun. He’s one of the best processors left in the league, and he’s a quarterback of an era gone by. It makes sense how he’d excel in this facet while other quarterbacks don’t have the same depth of background. Turnovers are primed for regression The path to winning MVP honors in the NFL is narrow. It takes only one bad game for the media to jump on board and derail a campaign. Stafford was able to stay the course and stave off the bad game. It also took a little luck for that to happen. According to PFF’s interception modeling, Stafford threw nearly seven fewer interceptions than expected. Two of these came from turnover-worthy plays (likely dropped interceptions, etc.) and 4.5 were purely good fortune through non-turnover-worthy throws where nothing went wrong (receivers batting well-thrown balls to defenders, etc.). While Stafford finished with single-digit interceptions with nine, he really should have been closer to 16 when all said and done. Additionally, opposing defenders dropped nine of Stafford’s would-be interceptions. This is additional “luck” that is not captured in the model. Appearances matter in MVP campaigns. Sometimes the stars need to align. They did for Stafford in 2025. That could all change in 2026 at no fault to the quarterback. This is an area where Stafford is due for regression. Perfectly accurate often, but not always consistent Stafford’ accuracy is a topic I have written about often. The analytics surrounding his performance in this area can be head-scratching. The QB Annual nails the strange juxtaposition. Stafford throws perfectly aimed passes as often as any other quarterback. He also misses throws at a rate that puts him towards the bottom of the NFL. While the Rams had one of the most explosive passing games in the league last year, they weren’t always efficient. Davante Adams received a very high volume of targets but on average caught just one of every two passes. LA is leaving a lot of meat on the bone. This is an area where they fortunes have potential to improve into the new year. In summary There are areas where we could likely see Stafford regress in 2026 only because of statistical probabilities. In the same vein, there are certainly areas where the Rams offense can take a notable step forward. The under center passing game is something McVay should expand on as Los Angeles continues to embrace heavier personnel packages. This is something Stafford uniquely does well and he’s the engine that makes the machine go. But Stafford could easily play just as well as he did last year only for his numbers and interception totals to be worse in 2026. That could single-handily derail another MVP campaign and could be enough to spoil LA’s Super Bowl expectations.
author: JB Scott

title: Max Klare aims to stand out in loaded Rams’ TE room
summary: The Los Angeles Rams have invested heavily in the tight end position in the last few seasons. Between Colby Parkinson, Tyler Higbee, second-year playmaker Terrance Ferguson and Davis Allen, rookie Max Klare is next in line to earn ample playing time in the Rams’ TE-heavy offense. Klare is L.A.’s second straight tight end selected in […]
full_text: Woodland Hills, - June 08:Rams Max Klare (86) at Rams practice on Monday, June 8, 2026. (Photo by David Crane/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams have invested heavily in the tight end position in the last few seasons. Between Colby Parkinson, Tyler Higbee, second-year playmaker Terrance Ferguson and Davis Allen, rookie Max Klare is next in line to earn ample playing time in the Rams’ TE-heavy offense. Klare is L.A.’s second straight tight end selected in the NFL draft, going No. 61 overall in April. This comes after Ferguson was taken 46th overall in last year’s draft. Klare is going to have his work cut out for him if he aims to stand out in this loaded grouping. He’ll certainly have an uphill climb. However, his versatile skills as a receiving TE — not to mention surviving the Purdue Boilermakers — could potentially make him stand out in the crowd. Moving from dreadful Boilermakers to greener pastures Klare attended St. Xavier in Cincinnati, Ohio, and committed to the Purdue Boilermakers out of high school as a three-star recruit. He chose the Boilermakers over schools like Duke, Eastern Michigan, Georgia Tech and the nearby Cincinnati Bearcats. Through his first two years at Purdue, nothing of note happened for the young tight end. He played in just two games during his freshman campaign in 2022. Then, the following year, he was on his way to potentially breaking out before suffering a season-ending injury in a 44-19 win over Illinois. Despite the injury, Klare was a dependable target in short-yardage situations. Purdue quarterback Hudson Card sung his praises to Sam King of the Lafayette Journal & Courier , a sign of something special to come in Year 3: “He’s one of the best tight ends that I’ve been around. He’s a great player. He can block and he also runs some of the best routes that I’ve been around. He makes my life easy and he’s going to do some special things.” Klare had the best season of his collegiate career in 2024, leading the team with 51 receptions for 685 yards and four touchdowns, which was the sixth-highest receiving yardage total by a TE in program history. According to Purdue Athletics , he finished eighth in the FBS in receiving yards by a tight end and was the ninth different Big Ten TE since 2000 to record at least 680 receiving yards. He returned from injury with a vengeance against FCS Indiana State in the season opener with a five-catch, 71-yard output. Later in the season, Klare also recorded a career-high 133 yards against the Fighting Illini. For his efforts, Klare was named third-team All-Big Ten. He would’ve likely gotten more respect from the voters had Purdue not performed so poorly that season. The Boilermakers finished 1-11 during his final season, including 0-9 in the Big Ten, lowlighted by 66-7 and 66-0 losses to in-state foes Notre Dame and Indiana, respectively. It was time for a change, and Klare opted to transfer to defending national champion Ohio State ahead of the 2025 season. While in Columbus, Klare worked to improve his blocking. Being with a contending program seemed to bring out his best, as he took quick notice of his improvement. The Buckeyes coasted through the regular season undefeated before back-to-back losses to Indiana in the Big Ten Championship and Miami in the College Football Playoff. Both of those teams faced off in the national championship, with the Hoosiers coming out on top. It was still a successful season for Klare, even if he missed out on the championship glory. He ended his lone year at Ohio State playing all 14 games , including 11 starts, finishing with 43 receptions for 448 yards and two touchdowns. Even with the slight dip in production compared to his final season at Purdue, he earned first-team all-Big Ten honors. Additionally, he had one year of eligibility remaining, but elected to enter the 2026 NFL draft. The Buckeyes’ loss will hopefully be the Rams’ gain. Klare might be lost in the crowd in Year 1 in Los Angeles Everybody knows the Rams like tight ends and cannot lie. That alone is a plus and a minus for the incoming Klare. On the plus side, Klare was drafted to the perfect team, one that utilizes multiple tight ends at any given time. Given L.A.’s commitment to the position, a receiving-first TE such as Klare will likely see the field more often than not. As for the minuses, for one, the Rams selected Ferguson in the second round of the 2025 NFL draft, which will give him priority on the field alongside veterans like Parkinson and Higbee. Ferguson played in 14 games last season, but wasn’t on the field as much as you’d think. The Oregon product started three of those 14 games and played just 39% of the offensive snaps in the regular season, per Pro Football Reference . Having a lot of mouths to feed is certainly a great problem to have as an offensive-minded coach like Sean McVay, but it’s also a problem for a rookie hoping to get playing time. Klare will undoubtedly be one of the Rams’ tight ends entering the season, yet where exactly he falls on the depth chart is undetermined. Overall. Klare doesn’t have a high ceiling as a blocker, which might hinder his time on the field, at least initially. While he did work on improving his blocking at Ohio State, The Athletic’s Dane Brugler cautioned that it will “likely never be a strength of his game”: “Klare has a low ceiling as a blocker and needs to continue adding refinement as a route runner, but his combination of athleticism, toughness and ball skills gives him a modern-day skill set. He projects as an F tight end, similar in ways to Dalton Kincaid.” A projection similar to Kincaid is a positive. He has been a serviceable target for Josh Allen for the last three years and has averaged just over 560 receiving yards since his selection in the 2023 NFL draft. Josh Norris and Hayden Winks of Yahoo Sports gave Klare an NFL comp of Cowboys two-time Pro Bowler Jake Ferguson in their breakdown of the Rams’ selection. If Klare can put up similar production to either of those tight ends during his first three years in Los Angeles, that would be the best possible outcome. All eyes will be on the Rams’ tight end room and how they’re utilized this season. Klare is only the team’s latest investment in the position, and one who the front office hopes will be a key cog for years to come.
author: Evan Craig

title: Raiders defense can’t afford to miss tackles in 2026 like last season
summary: Turning around a defense that was abysmal making sure tackles is a tall task for any defensive coordinator — let alone a rookie one. That’s where Rob Leonard finds himself with the Las Vegas Raiders. After impressing head coach Klint Kubiak and earning a promotion from defensive coach and run game coordinator to the Silver […]
full_text: Jun 3, 2026; Henderson, NV, USA; Las Vegas Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard speaks during a news conference during organized team activities at Intermountain Health Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Candice Ward-Imagn Images | Candice Ward-Imagn Images Turning around a defense that was abysmal making sure tackles is a tall task for any defensive coordinator — let alone a rookie one. That’s where Rob Leonard finds himself with the Las Vegas Raiders. After impressing head coach Klint Kubiak and earning a promotion from defensive coach and run game coordinator to the Silver & Black’s defensive coordinator, the 38-year-old is in charge of a group that ranked in the bottom five (or top five, depending on how you want to look at it) in missed tackles this past season. If there’s an incumbent coach that knows all too well the woes of Las Vegas’ defense, it’s Leonard. Let’s take a look at the numbers — from Pro Football Reference : By The Numbers Las Vegas Raiders Missed Tackles 2025 Team Total: 121 (5th most out of the 32 NFL teams) Leaders: LB Devin White 19; S Isaiah Pola-Mao 17, LB Elandon Roberts 11, S Jeremy Chinn 10, DT Jonah Laulu 10, DE Maxx Crosby 9, LB Jamal Adams 8 But let’s give credit where it is due: The 2025 performance was improvement over the 2024 campaign that saw then-defensive coordinator Patrick Graham’s unit ranked second overall in missed tackles with 134 total. That was behind the Indianapolis Colts’ 157 tally and ahead of the Carolina Panthers 132 total. But as you can see from the 121 whiffs Pro Football Reference charted the Raiders with in 2025, sure tackling remains an issue. And lo and behold, the Colts were in front of the Raiders with 125 missed tackles to take the fourth-most spot. For inquiring minds, the Cincinnati Bengals were far and away the whiff masters of the 2025 season with 170 missed tackles. As the Raiders embark on training camp under Kubiak’s watchful eye, let’s put it as blunt as I can: The team can’t afford to whiff on tackles this coming season like it did in year’s past. To help alleviate that and provide the rookie defensive coordinator ample talent, general manager John Spytek went to work this offseason bolstering the roster in free agency and the draft, all put Leonard in an advantageous position in his inaugural season as defensive boss. Quay Walker's 4.5% missed tackle rate was the 3rd lowest among linebackers with 100+ tackle attempts in 2025. His 28 yards allowed after missed tackles were the fewest in that group. @Raiders | #RaiderNation https://t.co/cZBzMI48PP pic.twitter.com/DPvjIdFf7c — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) March 9, 2026 The team’s poor tackling was a result of a three components and the struggles at the linebacker position was chief among them. The woes also includes scheme and technique breakdown and the lack of consistent pressure from the defensive front. Let’s kickoff with the linebacker spot. To say the linebacker position was an area of opportunity for the Silver & Black was a gross understatement. And the NFL Next Gen Stats post above is a prime example of shoring up deficiencies Las Vegas addressed this offseason. Quay Walker (three-year, $40.5 million contract) and Nakobe Dean (three-year, $30.6 million deal) are two high-priced additions the Raiders made to stock up a porous position group. Walker’s addition bodes well for shoring up the shoddy tackling due to ranking third according to NFL statistics tracking in missed tackle percentage. His collegiate teammate at Georgia, Dean, showcased the ability to make sure tackles as Pro Football Reference charted him with six missed tackles this past season while the group tracked Walker with five whiffs. Those totals are considerably lower than the digits above from the top Raiders offenders in 2025. The talent infusion should provide improvement over the group helmed by Graham that yielded a league-high 416 yards after missed tackles. Because on paper, Walker and Dean provide upgrades from Devin White and Elandon Roberts. Let’s shift to scheme and technique. This is where Leonard will sink or swim. Early returns are encouraging for the Raiders, though. Like the head coach who elevated him, Leonard is a stickler for the small things and attention to detail is a core tenet. Raiders defenders consistently took poor angles and relied way too much on either arm tackles or hard hits instead of wrapping up securely for stops, the past two seasons. And Leonard’s philosophy should cleanse the defense from its habitual brain farts due to his intense but focused coaching style built to instill confidence and composure. The style of play Leonard expects from his defense also looms large. New #Raiders DC Rob Leonard on his vision for the defense: "Style of play, man. I'm going to coach the defense like I coached the D-line. I still do the same things I do… A product on the field that you know what it looks like… All those little things outside the scheme is… pic.twitter.com/2ulSBYEn2j — Nick Walters (@nickwalt) June 3, 2026 Implementing an aggressive 3-4 defensive front that requires the 11 defenders to swarm to the ball, Leonard is concocting a defense that is the quintessential “see ball, get ball” group. The shift to an attacking 3-4 base defense that’s designed to stymie the run and send an array of rushers at the quarterback when opportunities present themselves, the Raiders want to be physical, fast, and to the point where flying to the ball with reckless abandon is welcomed — even at the cost of mental errors. And this is where we explore the third of the trio of issues in the tackling department: Pressure and the lack of it. By playing with an attacking attitude and maintaining that until the final whistle, Las Vegas sets the initiative. In previous seasons, the Raiders played more of a read-and-react style that often resembled the bend-but-don’t-break philosophy. This isn’t to say the team didn’t blitz. Under Graham, the team did it’s fair share of that. But the absence of complementary havoc creators alongside edge rusher Maxx Crosby was just as glaring as the absence of quality talent at the linebacker spots. According to Pro Football Reference, the Raiders generated 115 total pressures on opposing quarterbacks and just 34 hurries in 2025. That netted the Silver & Black the fifth and third worst rankings in both categories. To help add more teeth to the pass rush, Spytek brough in a power-type edge rusher in Kwity Paye (three-year, $48 million contract) in free agency and according to NFL.com writer Matt Okada, the former Indianapolis Colt logged 40-plus pressures in each of the last three seasons before coming to Las Vegas . The following month int he 2026 NFL Draft, the Raiders added Auburn defensive end Keyron Crawford in the third round, a supremely gifted athletic but unrefined edge rusher who has a high ceiling and is moldable (similar to Crosby back in the day). Mix the blitz-adept and aggressive Dean to that mix and Leonard’s front seven should do a lot more attacking the offense than reacting to what the offense is doing. And playing with momentum forward is a heck of a lot better than a defense playing on its heels and, as a result, whiffing on tackles.

Two is definitely sufficient considering we’re gonna be more of a run attack style offense so with that being said, I think this team can surprise a lot of teams considering they don’t have any film on this offense this quarterback, this new coaching staff so I think if our coaches can actually coach we should be able to win 10 to 12 games with a young healthy roster and let me put things in perspective for most of you people out there the critics if you will if you’re in the NFL you can play football. title: Everson Griffen Says He’s Looking For An NFL Comeback
summary: With the official start of training camp for the Minnesota Vikings coming this week, we’re sure to hear a lot about guys being in the best shape of their careers, taking it one day at a time, and (insert your favorite offseason cliché right here). However, we may now be hearing it from someone that […]
full_text: With the official start of training camp for the Minnesota Vikings coming this week, we’re sure to hear a lot about guys being in the best shape of their careers, taking it one day at a time, and (insert your favorite offseason cliché right here). However, we may now be hearing it from someone that a lot of us may not have thought about in a while. In an interview with Josina Anderson, former Vikings pass-rushing star Everson Griffen says that he wants to make a comeback into the National Football League. His interview with Anderson is about an hour long, and you can see the whole thing in this YouTube video. In the interview, Griffen talks about reaching one year of sobriety (congratulations to him on that mark), as well as his bipolar disorder, among other topics. His off-field issues aside, the deck would appear to be stacked against Griffen making a comeback in the NFL for a couple of significant reasons. The first reason is that he’s 39 years old. Not to say that players can’t be productive in the NFL when they reach their late 30s or anything like that. After all, Chris Doleman came back to the Vikings for one last season when he was 38 years old and put up eight sacks before announcing his retirement. The much bigger issue is the fact that Griffen hasn’t set foot on an NFL field since Week 11 of the 2021 season, nearly five full years ago. That was in his second tour of duty with the Vikings and, if you’ll recall, it was after that game that the Vikings placed him on the Non-Football Illness list following a mental health incident at his home. That ended his 2021 season and, though we didn’t know it at the time, ended that chapter of his NFL career. Griffen says that he can be ready in three months. The start of the NFL regular season is about seven weeks or so away, so if he truly is in a position to make a comeback, it won’t be until late September/early October at the earliest. Don’t get me wrong, I want to wish Everson Griffen the best of luck if he has all of his personal issues sorted out and wants to try to get back onto the gridiron again. I’m just not totally sure how much we should make of it or expect from it, honestly.

title: Will Campbell carrying lessons from NFL vets into Patriots training camp
summary: New England Patriots left tackle and 2025 first-round draft selection Will Campbell took advantage of opportunities outside of the organization this offseason, training with NFL veterans in Dallas, he told media members on Sunday. “A ton of knowledge,” Will Campbell said after Sunday’s practice about what he took away from the experience. “I work with […]
full_text: Jun 10, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots offensive tackle Will Campbell (66) does a drill with offensive tackle Lorenz Metz (72) during minicamp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images New England Patriots left tackle and 2025 first-round draft selection Will Campbell took advantage of opportunities outside of the organization this offseason, training with NFL veterans in Dallas, he told media members on Sunday. “A ton of knowledge,” Will Campbell said after Sunday’s practice about what he took away from the experience. “I work with a lot of guys who have been around a long time and done it at a high level for a long time. So just anything that they could teach me that could help me. “Or whether that’s football or off the field, or just training and just being around in the same environment. I always want to put myself in the best position possible.” Lane Johnson, Tristan Wirfs, Rashawn Slater and New York Jets 2025 first-round pick Armand Membou invited Campbell south of Foxboro, where the group trained with the world’s strongest man, Mitchell Hooper, and a former Navy SEAL. While training, Campbell strengthened his relationships with the veterans who were present, saying he feels that he can always reach out to them if needed. Before traveling to Dallas, the 22-year-old told the media during voluntary OTAs that he underwent physical therapy five days a week throughout the offseason to recover from a torn MCL in 2025. Campbell suffered the injury during Week 12 against the Cincinnati Bengals. Still, the second-year lineman quickly returned for New England’s postseason run, but his effectiveness dipped during those final five contests. In his first 12 games last season, Campbell posted a 76.1 pass-blocking grade on Pro Football Focus ; however, that number drastically decreased to 39.2 following the injury. Entering training camp, the LSU product said he’s feeling “great” when asked about his recovery. “It’s exciting,” Campbell said about being back in Foxboro. “[It’s] good to be back. Good to see everybody. [I’m] excited about what we have, and I’m ready to go.” One of Campbell’s goals for the summer sessions is to further build his chemistry with starting left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker, who was signed to a multi-year deal in free agency . Though the two are still early in that process, as Vera-Tucker was limited in his participation through most of the spring, recovering from a torn triceps. “Just continue to grow every day,” Campbell said of his goals. “Just me and [Alijah Vera-Tucker] continuing to get comfortable playing next to each other and just doing my job to the best of my ability.” The left-side tandem will look to build on the Patriots’ offensive line improvement from 2025.

title: Mack Hollins embracing fierce competition in Patriots’ wide receiver room
summary: Mack Hollins lives for competition. That’s why training camp is his favorite time of the year. “We’re ball players. You got to love being out here,” Hollins said after the team’s training camp practice on Sunday. “This is my favorite time of the year because you’re competing and everybody’s competing at the highest level to […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Mack Hollins (13) waits his turn to do a drill at minicamp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images Mack Hollins lives for competition. That’s why training camp is his favorite time of the year. “We’re ball players. You got to love being out here,” Hollins said after the team’s training camp practice on Sunday . “This is my favorite time of the year because you’re competing and everybody’s competing at the highest level to earn a job. Not that guys aren’t competing during the season, but practice can be separated into different things and becomes looks for the next team you’re playing against, but training camp is like everybody’s bringing their best and we’re both lining up to win. “So, I love it. I love the schedule. I love wall-to-wall ball. I love staying in a hotel. I don’t know. I guess that’s just me.” The competition is especially fierce inside his wide receiver room this year. A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs were added to the top of the depth chart, while Hollins joins Kayshon Boutte, DeMario Douglas, Kyle Williams, and Efton Chism III in competing for snaps behind them. For Hollins, the talent around him is simply more motivation. “I think it’s the iron sharpens iron kind of mentality,” Hollins said. “You get a lot of great guys in one room. All you can do is get better, or you get left behind. And I think what I’ve seen so far — it’s been two days, plus OTAs — but really two days is this room just is like, ‘all right, cool. We’re all just gonna get better then. We’re gonna find out who’s the best.’ Everybody might have an idea of who should be here, who should be here, but we’re all, ‘hey, it’s all a clean slate. You got to earn your spot.’” In his first season with the Patriots, Hollins led all New England wide receivers playing 68% of the offensive snaps. His 46 receptions and 550 yards were his highest totals since 2022, when he first played under offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels in Las Vegas. Now entering Year 10 and his second season in New England, Hollins has tried to turn back the clock in order to make sure he is the one who does not get left behind. “I think I’ve actually kind of gone back to what I used to be,” Hollins said. “I think it’s easy to get comfortable in how camp is. It’s easy, like, you’ve been doing it a long time, just stay with the flow. And I’ve tried to go back to being young and being just so hungry to learn stuff, acting like I’ve never seen this offense before, lifting hard, running hard, chasing down plays, doing more work than anybody after practice, like doing all those things, because you got to remember to go back to chopping wood. “It’s easy to just be like, ‘I’m good.’ Like these guys, I already know the offense. I’ve been with Josh for a culmination of probably four years altogether in my career, five years. So going back to what I originally was and what got me here.” So far, the approach has worked for the 32-year-old, as Hollins feels he has another 10 years in him. “Yeah, I’m halfway there. I got 10 more in me,” Hollins said. “So if they can stop me, then maybe I’ll stop early. But they haven’t stopped me.”

full_text: Foxborough, MA - June 11: New England Patriots defensive tackle Christian Barmore at minicamp on June 11, 2026. (Photo by Barry Chin/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images Vince Wilfork knows a thing or two about defensive line play in the NFL. A New England Patriots Hall of Famer, he helped the team win two Super Bowls and was one of the best nose tackles of his era. Even in retirement he continues to have a positive impact on the team, albeit more subtly. As current Patriots defensive tackle Christian Barmore revealed during his training camp media availability on Sunday , Wilfork is regularly reaching out to him to get him fired up for game day. “Every time it’s game day, he’ll hit me up and say, ‘Hey man, you have to set the tone every time,’” Barmore revealed. “He just gets me fired up every time. He’s a legend. He’s one of the best players to ever play the game. So every time he texts me or just hits me up, it’s a blessing because he’s a legend. It motivates me every time I see that message.” For Barmore, his connection with Wilfork is about more than just motivating text messages. It’s about knowing that even in his sixth year in the league, he is not a fully-developed player yet. “I still learn every day. Of course, nobody is perfect,” the 26-year-old said. “My mission is to get guys that need help, I’m going to help them out. I always tell them, ask coach, or ask anybody that played the game long. I talk to Big Vince when I need to, or I talk to legends like Coach T[errell Williams] or Coach [Mike] Vrabel. The guys, they are not afraid to tell me what I need to work on and need to keep being the best I can be for the team.” A second-round draft choice by the Patriots in 2021, Barmore quickly became a mainstay along the team’s interior defensive line. One of the most disruptive D-linemen in the league, he signed a four-year, $84 million contract extension in 2024 but shortly thereafter found himself sidelined due to blood clots. Barmore eventually made his way back, with 2025 his first full season after his recovery. He appeared in all 21 games and finished with three combined sacks. Now, he is looking is to take another step in his development, and — just like Vince Wilfork is doing for him — help. bring the younger guys along as well. “Keep coming out here, set an example for my guys, the young guys, and just showing the proof every day,” he explained. “Keep getting better every day, and just keep balling, keep doing good.”

title: Monday could bring movement to the Christian Gonzalez contract stalemate
summary: If Robert Kraft is to be believed, the New England Patriots are fully prepared to make Christian Gonzalez the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history. So, what’s the holdup? One belief is that the Patriots want to wait for the Seattle Seahawks to first finalize a contract extension with their own 2023 first-round cornerback, Devon Witherspoon. […]
full_text: Jul 25, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez (0) and owner Robert Kraft attend training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images If Robert Kraft is to be believed, the New England Patriots are fully prepared to make Christian Gonzalez the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history . So, what’s the holdup? One belief is that the Patriots want to wait for the Seattle Seahawks to first finalize a contract extension with their own 2023 first-round cornerback, Devon Witherspoon. With Witherspoon as the benchmark, the Patriots would then know where to set Gonzalez’s own deal to indeed make him the top-earning CB in football. If so, Monday could be a big day. By the end of the business day, after all, roster bonuses embedded into first-round rookie contracts are due to be paid. For the Patriots, three such players qualify , including Gonzalez: the fourth-year defender is set to see his bank account go up by $550,000. Witherspoon is also in that group for the Seahawks, and his bonus is a lot higher on the basis of him being selected 12 draft picks before Gonzalez: it’s worth roughly $3.95 million. The Seahawks can easily fit that number under their cap — in fact, it already is part of the calculations. The question is whether or not they want it to be paid out as a lump-sum rather than spread over the duration of a potential new deal. With such a deal rumored to be close, John Gilbert of SB Nation’s Seahawks blog, Field Gulls , argues that Seattle might be motivated to push the Witherspoon extension over the line on Monday: [B]ecause the bonus becomes earned Monday, at that point the associated $3,949,702 2026 cap charge connected to the bonus becomes locked in and would not be impacted by a extension between the two sides. In contrast, if the two sides reach agreement on an extension prior to Monday, the roster bonus could be wrapped into a signing bonus, allowing for a small bit of cash flow to be pushed into the future, along with part of the cap hit, which would potentially reduce the 2026 cash obligations of the team. … Now, certainly the Seahawks can afford to pay in either scenario, but almost any business owner who has the option on whether to spend $26,145,000 instead of $30,094,702 now with the difference being paid at some point in the future will opt for the lower amount. While the motivation itself might be speculative, the numbers are not. Could they be enough to spur the Seahawks into action? It at least seems possible, because even soft deadlines can have a certain power to them. In turn, the Patriots-Gonzalez stalemate might also finally see some movement. Although it seems unlikely that New England worries too much about the roster bonus, in part because it is only a fraction of Witherspoon’s, anything happening in Seattle appears to be of interest to the organization and Gonzalez’s representatives. Monday could therefore be quite a big stop on the road toward the 24-year-old becoming the highest-paid cornerback in the game and officially a long-term Patriot.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: What moving Jeremiah Webb to IR after Gabe Jacas signing means for the Patriots
summary: It did not take the New England Patriots long to suffer their first season-ending injury of training camp. On Sunday, after he had suffered what looked like a non-serious injury in the previous day’s practice, Jeremiah Webb was placed on the injured reserve list. The move puts a premature end to the wide receiver’s sophomore […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2025; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Jeremiah Webb (29) warms up during minicamp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images It did not take the New England Patriots long to suffer their first season-ending injury of training camp. On Sunday, after he had suffered what looked like a non-serious injury in the previous day’s practice , Jeremiah Webb was placed on the injured reserve list . The move puts a premature end to the wide receiver’s sophomore season. What else does it mean for the Patriots, though? Let’s find out. Second shoe dropped When the news broke on Saturday that Gabe Jacas had agreed to his rookie contract with the Patriots, the clock started ticking. Once he had officially signed the deal , the Patriots needed to make space for him on their active 90-man offseason roster (which actually stands at 91 due to the presence of roster-exempt offensive tackle Lorenz Metz). They did so by moving Webb to IR. That transaction was already preceded by New England already bolstering its wide receiver group through claiming Kobe Prentice off waivers on Saturday. WR room back to 11 Prentice joining the Patriots on Saturday temporarily increased the number of wide receivers on the Patriots’ roster to 12. With Webb now on injured reserve, it is back down to 11: W. de receiver (11): A.J. Brown (1), Romeo Doubs (87), DeMario Douglas (3), Kayshon Boutte (9), Mack Hollins (13), Kyle Williams (18), Efton Chism III (86), Kyle Dixon (83), Nick DeGennaro (23), Cameron Dorner (88), Kobe Prentice (19) IR (2): Jeremiah Webb, Jimmy Kibble Webb now joins Jimmy Kibble on injured reserve; the undrafted rookie was waived with an injury designation on the eve of training camp and subsequently reverted to IR after going unclaimed. In total, the Patriots now have three players on IR: Webb, Kibble and tight end Julian Hill. Limited impact Webb was one of the feel-good stories of last year’s training camp. Signed as a rookie free agent, who had joined the Berlin Thunder of the European League of Football even before the 2025 NFL Draft had taken place, he delivered multiple quality performances in training camp and preseason to earn himself a spot on New England’s practice squad for the 2025 season. Entering his second year in the system, however, his outlook was murky. The Patriots had invested some serious resources in their wide receiver group over the offseason, and Webb found himself facing an uphill battle for the roster. The practice squad was not a given either considering that the team had also added four undrafted rookies to the mix as well. From a pure football perspective, therefore, Webb’s season ending in late July is unlikely to have a major impact on the fortunes of New England’s passing game in 2026. Cap changes Moving Webb to injured reserve actually has no impact on New England’s salary cap at the moment. With a salary of $885,000 and no guarantees in his deal, he did not count against the team’s books under the Top 51 rule. However, his split salary of $515,000 will become relevant once said rule is lifted before the regular season begins. Even with Webb’s move off the active roster not directly changing the Patriots’ cap yet, it looks different today than it did 24 hours ago. The reason for that is Jacas signing his rookie contract: his combined cap number of $1.57 million does qualify for Top 51 status and therefore pushes a lower-salaried player — there are actually six that have identical $1.08 million cap hits — from the list. This results in a net cap space loss of $498,994. Edge questions remain Let’s briefly close on Jacas. While him signing his rookie contract is without doubt a positive development, the questions about New England’s edge position remain now that he has been placed on NFI. With him and Harold Landry both on injury lists now, two of the projected top three players at the position — all but free agency pickup Dre’Mont Jones — are now sidelined for medical reasons. Obviously, Jacas and Landry can both return at any point. How quickly they are brought up to speed once that happens, however, is unclear.

title: Patriots place receiver on injured reserve, add second-rounder Gabe Jacas to NFI list
summary: After one last unsigned draft pick agreed to terms at Gillette Stadium, another roster move loomed to make room. The New England Patriots opened a 91-man spot on Sunday by placing wide receiver Jeremiah Webb on injured reserve. Barring an injury settlement at a later date, the transaction ends the sophomore’s campaign just two practices […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Jeremiah Webb (29) runs after making a catch at minicamp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images After one last unsigned draft pick agreed to terms at Gillette Stadium, another roster move loomed to make room. The New England Patriots opened a 91-man spot on Sunday by placing wide receiver Jeremiah Webb on injured reserve. Barring an injury settlement at a later date, the transaction ends the sophomore’s campaign just two practices into training camp. Webb, 25, entered the NFL as part of New England’s 2025 undrafted class. After catching six passes for 80 yards and one touchdown during his rookie preseason, the 5-foot-11, 198-pound wideout and returner was waived at the 53-man roster deadline last August. He went through the league wire unclaimed and proceeded to join the organization’s practice squad at its formation. From there, Webb served as an inactive standard elevation for January’s wild card versus the Los Angeles Chargers and reached a futures contract following Super Bowl LX. The former transfer from South Dakota to South Alabama now no longer counts against the club’s active limit. In a precursor on Sunday, the Patriots announced the signing of outside linebacker Gabe Jacas, the No. 55 overall pick in the 2026 class, to his four-year, $8.6 million rookie contract. Yet to practice, the Illinois product has since been moved to the active/non-football injury list alongside running back Terrell Jennings and special teams captain Brenden Schooler. All three on the NFI list are eligible to begin practicing at any point during training camp. The same holds true for tight end C.J. Dippre and veteran edge Harold Landry III, who currently reside on New England’s physically unable to perform . The team will hold a walkthrough at 10 a.m. ET on Monday.

title: Dre’Mont Jones sees bright future for Patriots’ young, underrated pass rush
summary: To many, the New England Patriots’ edge group carries the most questions on the roster. Head coach Mike Vrabel, however, has stood by his current group when asked about the position both this spring and at the start of training camp.  One of those players, veteran Dre’Mont Jones, agrees. “I think we’re an underrated group, […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - May 27: New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel works with linebacker Dre'Mont Jones on May 27, 2026. (Photo by John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images To many, the New England Patriots’ edge group carries the most questions on the roster. Head coach Mike Vrabel, however, has stood by his current group when asked about the position both this spring and at the start of training camp. One of those players, veteran Dre’Mont Jones, agrees. “I think we’re an underrated group, and the world’s going to see how good we can be,” he said. Jones was signed to a three-year, $39.5 million contract on the first day of free agency to bolster the Patriots’ pass rush and run defense along the edge. Coming off of a career season that included seven sacks, the 29-year old will join Harold Landry III atop the depth chart once the veteran is activated off the PUP list. Behind them, however, is young group that is led by Elijah Ponder, Bradyn Swinson, and second-round draft pick Gabe Jacas, who officially signed his rookie contract on Sunday. One of those young edge rushers emerging would be a welcome development for the Patriots this summer. And through his early time with Ponder and Swinson, Jones believes both have the potential to make that leap. “Elijah, he can be the truth… He’s going to be a helluva player. I think Pats Nation got a steal,” Jones said. “Swinson, he can be a killer in this league. “How they work and how talented they are. They are a smart young couple of players who understand the game. How they elevate is based upon them, but they definitely have the building blocks to be great.” While Sunday’s practice was a positive one for the defense, New England’s defensive front has not yet fully gotten in on the fun — outside of a pair of batted passes from Jones and Swinson — throughout the non-padded sessions. That should change once the pads come on, something veteran safety Kevin Byard is eager to see. “When the pads come on days into training camp, I expect those guys to start making a lot more plays,” he said. “But defense, we’ve been having a lot of fun the first couple days.”

title: 5 performances of note from the Patriots’ second training camp practice
summary: The New England Patriots held their second training camp practice of the summer on Sunday morning. Attendance was again good, the weather was nice, and the action was plentiful. If you want to recap it, please make sure to check out our daily practice recap. In the meantime, here are the players that caught our […]
full_text: Jul 25, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots tight end Tanner Arkin (84) walks to the practice field at training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images The New England Patriots held their second training camp practice of the summer on Sunday morning. Attendance was again good, the weather was nice, and the action was plentiful. If you want to recap it, please make sure to check out our daily practice recap . In the meantime, here are the players that caught our eye for better or worse. Standout of the day The pass defense: We couldn’t just name one player from the Patriots’ pass defense today because the unit as a whole performed at a high level. Whether it was Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis providing tight coverage throughout the day and both breaking up passes, John Saunders Jr. registering a PBU on a deep attempt from Behren Morten, or Milton Williams getting his hands up to bat a Drake Maye attempt incomplete at the line of scrimmage, the unit came to play on Sunday. It’s most notable moment, however, was the first interception of the summer. Drake Maye attempted to hit A.J. Brown on a deep crossing route, but threw a bit too high, which led to the wide receiver simply tipping the pass. The deflection landed right in the waiting arms of Craig Woodson for the pick. Woodson, like the rest of the Patriots’ secondary, was around the ball quite a bit during the session. It’s early, of course, but this defensive backfield is going to be fun to watch this season. Other performances of note QB Behren Morton: Entering training camp, the Patriots’ pecking order at quarterback appeared set in stone. And while that still looks to be the case after two practices, Morton is performing quite well as the third-stringer. On Sunday, he completed five of his six passes in team drills — the lone incompletion being the deep ball mentioned above — and was confident operating the unit and showed some creativity in the pocket. WR Nick DeGennaro: Working with the third-string unit, DeGennaro had an active day in team drills. The undrafted free agent finished the session with multiple receptions from the aforementioned Behren Morton, and looked like the most reliable target in the young QB’s arsenal. He’s still a long way from pushing for a roster spot, but he did perform well on Sunday. TE Tanner Arkin: The Patriots added Arkin as a rookie free agent after the draft, and just three months later he is getting reps with the first-team offense. He saw action as a blocking tight end, and not just that: with Reggie Gilliam a surprise absentee, Arkin also lined up as a fullback. In addition, he practiced some long-snapping alongside Julian Ashby. While the full-pads sessions will show just how good his chanced of making the roster ultimately are, Sunday appeared to be a step in the right direction for the 23-year-old. K Andy Borregales: After not seeing any action on Saturday, the Patriots’ sophomore attempted six kicks during a field goal period. Working from a distance between roughly 30 and 50 yards, Borregales split the uprights on all six of them and looked mightily comfortable in the process. The Patriots will hold their third practice of training camp on Monday. Gates will open at 9:15 p.m. ET with the session set to start approximately an hour later.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots training camp recap: Pass defense wins the day
summary: The New England Patriots held their second practice of training camp on Sunday on the practice fields behind Gillette Stadium. The 90-minute session did not feature any pads and contact remained limited as they continue to ramp things up. Here’s what went down throughout the day. Attendance Absentees: ED Gabe Jacas, WR Jeremiah Webb (new), […]
full_text: Jul 25, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots safety Craig Woodson (4) makes a catch at training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images The New England Patriots held their second practice of training camp on Sunday on the practice fields behind Gillette Stadium. The 90-minute session did not feature any pads and contact remained limited as they continue to ramp things up. Here’s what went down throughout the day. Attendance Absentees: ED Gabe Jacas, WR Jeremiah Webb (new), FB Reggie Gilliam (new) PUP/NFI: RB Terrell Jennings, TE C.J. Dippre, ED Harold Landry III, S Brenden Schooler Injuries: N/A Edge rusher Gabe Jacas was in the building to sign his rookie contract on Sunday but did not yet join the team on the practice field as he works back from several pre-drafty injuries. Reggie Gilliam was a new absence in addition to Jeremiah Webb, who was slightly banged up to end Saturday’s session . All four players then remained on PUP/NFI lists. Takeaways Pass defense shines: After the Patriots’ offense struck its fair share of explosives to open camp, New England’s defense punched back on Sunday. That was highlighted by the first interception of camp, as a high pass intended for A.J. Brown over the middle of the field tipped off the receiver’s outstretched finger tips and was corralled by Craig Woodson. The Patriots pass defense didn’t stop there, as Christian Gonzalez, who was again a full participant, and Carlton Davis recorded pass breakups of their own. Milton Williams even got into the action batting a pass down at the line of scrimmage. Drake’s inaccuracies: The miss to Brown was not the only overthrow of the day for Drake Maye. The quarterback’s first pass of the afternoon saw him miss Hunter Henry high on a crosser, while Maye also overthrow an open Eli Raridon later off a play-action bootleg with a free rusher chasing him from behind. Boutte’s big play: A day after making the highlight play of the day, Kayshon Boutte was on scene again to provide the Patriots’ offense their largest play of Sunday’s session. Working against Carlton Davis, Boutte worked the sideline nicely to haul in a back shoulder ball from Maye for a roughly 20-yard gain. Elsewhere at wide receiver, Maye and Brown connected for the first time in camp on a simple slant route. Maye’s lone target to Romeo Doubs on the day was incomplete. Mack Hollins and Kyle Williams, who ran a strong downfield comeback route, got their first catches of the summer from Tommy DeVito. UDFA Nick DeGennaro then got on the board with two catches from Behren Morton. Lomu’s snaps: With veteran right tackle Morgan Moses not taking any competitive reps on Sunday, first rounder Caleb Lomu repped in his place. The Patriots also got Lomu reps as the jumbo tight end where they would then insert Marcus Bryant at right tackle with Lomu eligible. The rest of the Patriots offensive line remained the same with Will Campbell, Alijah Vera-Tucker, Jared Wilson, and Mike Onwenu filling the other four spots. The lone procedural blemish appeared to be a false start on Vera-Tucker. Other notes: It was another impressive showing for rookie quarterback Behren Morton is his limited work. Morton continues to look comfortable stepping up and navigating in the pocket. Lan Larison was again the first running back to receive a carry behind TreVeyon Henderson and Rhamondre Stevenson. While it’s tough to judge running backs in these settings (especially with no pads), Jam Miller had some strong moments. Eli Raridon continued to be used in 12 personnel packages next to Hunter Henry and was open on an overthrow by Maye. DeVito also missed the rookie high before later connecting. Also in the tight end room, UDFA Tanner Arkin got a run with the first unit as a pseudo fullback with Gilliam sidelined. He also took some warmup reps as a long snapper alongside Julian Ashby at one point. While contact is limited in these settings, both Christian Elliss and Jesse Luketa drew a reaction from the crowd for plays on running backs. After Mike Brown served as the big nickel on Saturday, safety Dell Pettus took over that role Sunday alongside Craig Woodson and Kevin Byard. Andy Borregales went 6-for-6 in his first field goal period of the summer, with distances appearing to range from 30 to 50 yards. The Patriots will be back on the practice fields on Monday for Day 3 of camp which is set to be a walkthrough that starts at 10 a.m. ET. Head coach Mike Vrabel will speak beforehand.

title: 5 ‘things I think’ on the eve of NY Giants training camp
summary: New York Giants players report for training camp on Tuesday, with practice starting on Wednesday. Here are some of the things I am thinking about as a new season of Giants football, the first with 18-year veteran head coach John Harbaugh at the wheel, dawns. That Harbaugh speech The John Harbaugh “This is the New […]
full_text: John Harbaugh | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images New York Giants players report for training camp on Tuesday, with practice starting on Wednesday. Here are some of the things I am thinking about as a new season of Giants football, the first with 18-year veteran head coach John Harbaugh at the wheel, dawns. That Harbaugh speech The John Harbaugh “This is the New York Giants” speech to his team on their first day together has drawn criticism . I think that criticism is stupid and misguided. The Giants are one of the league’s iconic original franchises. They have won eight championships — four Super Bowls and four titles in the pre-Super Bowl era. Harbaugh was reminding players of what the franchise has been, of the legacy they should embrace and strive to emulate. He wasn’t simply blowing rah-rah smoke. Players and assistant coaches have all lauded Harbaugh’s daily messages to the team. To take one small snippet, without hearing the rest of Harbaugh’s message, and twist it into something “cringey” or to be made fun of is nonsense. “The New York Giants. The New York Giants! This is the New York Giants sitting in this room! The New York Giants” Starting to think John Harbaugh is pumped to be on the Giants pic.twitter.com/IJoTmK7dor — Barstool Sports (@barstoolsports) July 22, 2026 Handling a Harbaugh camp I am extremely curious to see how much of a shock Harbaugh’s training camp, which promises more physicality and less coddling than many NFL players have become accustomed to, is to the players. Media, too. It certainly promises to be interesting. Tight end Isaiah Likely was with Harbaugh for the past four years with the Baltimore Ravens. He says he has been “institutionalized”. “With Coach Harbs, this is all I ever know,” Likely said. “Whatever he’s doing at practice, I’ve been doing it for the last four years in a row. So, whatever you all see out there is what you’re going to get every time.” We saw some indications of Harbaugh’s ways in the spring. Draft picks took snaps during rookie mini-camp, something Giants’ draft picks had not done in several years. Spring practices ran as long as the Collective Bargaining Agreement would allow. The Giants did 9-on-7 run drills without pads, an unusual sight. First- and second-team players took more reps than we have become accustomed to seeing. The West Virginia schedule is an indication things will be different. The Giants will practice for four days, take Sunday off, then practice six consecutive days. I can’t remember the last time a Giants team did that. And I’m not Dan Duggan of The Athletic, who probably has that detail tucked away in a years-old notebook somewhere. Position battles We probably already know about 75% of the 53-man roster , maybe a little more than that. There are competitions for both roster spots and playing time that will be worth watching. Here are the five battles I think I am most interested: CB2 — Will the starting cornerback opposite Paulson Adebo be behind door Number 1 (Greg Newsome), Door No. 2 (Colton Hood), or Door No. 3 (Deonte Banks)? Defensive line — If you know who, out of Zacch Pickens, Sam Roberts, Josh Futou, Bobby Jamison-Travis, Leki Fotu, Ben Barten, and Anquin Barnes Jr. is going to make the roster, you are smarter than I am. Wide receiver — Can Odell Beckham make the roster? If he can’t, who does? Is this finally the end of the line for Jalin Hyatt? Offensive line — Who will the Giants keep as their backups? Would they dare try to pass J.C. Davis through waivers and get him to the practice squad? Can Evan Neal somehow earn a spot? Will Jon Runyan face real competition for the left guard job? Safety — This is not really about roster spots. I want to know if either Ar’Darius Washington or Jason Pinnock can take Tyler Nubin’s starting job. Malik Nabers’ progress Nabers, coming back from a pair of surgeries to fix a torn ACL, will avoid the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list at the beginning of camp. How much he does each day, and how he looks while doing it, is going to become a daily. I would suspect a slow ramp-up for Nabers designed to, hopefully, get him to full speed for Week 1 against the Dallas Cowboys. I would expect Nabers to do more than warm-up drills and perhaps some individual drills early in camp. Perhaps some 7-on-7 and 1-on-1 work as camp moves along, and some 11-on-11 action later in camp. I’d guess there is no chance Nabers plays in a preseason game. A long way from home Truthfully, as I have thought about this column over the past several days, and tried to chisel out time to write it, I have been distracted by my own thoughts about and preparations for spending the next two weeks in West Virginia. I report to West Virginia for camp on Monday, and have been pre-occupied for days with thoughts of what I needed to do before leaving, and all of the things I needed to bring. I’ve resigned myself to having a couple of “oh, s—-, I didn’t bring such and such” with me moments. It is a 586-mile drive from my home to my accommodations for 12 nights. I am grateful for the opportunity to cover this important stretch for the Giants in person — I have always believed seeing things with my own eyes is the only way to do this job corectly. Still, this will be the longest stretch of time ever spent away from my bride of 41 years (as of Aug. 10). I might miss the birth of our fourth grandchild, unless the little man cooperates and waits for grandpa to get home. I would, though, feel like I wasn’t doing my job properly if I wasn’t there. I hope you enjoy, and benfit from, the coverage here at Big Blue View of the West Virginia chapter of the upcoming season. Let the adventure begin!

title: NY Giants training camp 53-man roster projection: Locks, bubble players, longshots
summary: Instead of doing a pure 53-man roster projection ahead of New York Giants training camp, which begins Wednesday in West Virginia, here is a different way to break down the 91-man roster. Below is a position-by-position look at who I consider to be locks to make the 53-man roster, bubble players, and long shots. The […]
full_text: Odell Beckham | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Instead of doing a pure 53-man roster projection ahead of New York Giants training camp, which begins Wednesday in West Virginia, here is a different way to break down the 91-man roster. Below is a position-by-position look at who I consider to be locks to make the 53-man roster, bubble players, and long shots. The intent is to look at where the most interesting competitions are and the chances of individual players. Quarterback Locks (2) — Jaxson Dart, Jameis Winston Bubble players (0) — None Long shot (1) — Brandon Allen I don’t see the Giants keeping a third quarterback on the roster. Allen wasn’t good this spring, but he is an experienced player with ties to quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan. If an upgrade doesn’t fall into the Giants’ lap, keeping Allen on the practice squad is fine. Running back Locks (4) — Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy, Devin Singletary, Patrick Ricard Bubble players (0) — None Long shots (3) — Eric Gray, Dante Miller, Damon Bankston Maybe Gray, Miller, and Bankston should be in the “bubble” category rather than the “long shots” category. No matter. Entering camp, I don’t think any of them are making the 53-man roster if Skattebo, Tracy, and Singletary are healthy. Bankston, 23, probably has the best chance. He is 23, Gray 26, and Miller 27. Age and upside favor the undrafted free agent. Tight end Locks (3) — Isaiah Likely, Theo Johnson, Chris Manhertz Bubble players (1) — Thomas Fidone Long shot (1) — Tanner Conner During our training camp preview podcast, Patty Traina of Giants on SI floated the idea that the Giants would keep just two tight ends — Likely and Johnson — because of the presence of Ricard [ 20:03 mark ]. I’m not buying. With as many two-tight-end and heavy sets as I expect to see from the Giants this season, I can’t see them having only two true tight ends active. Manhertz remains a quality blocker and veteran leader. I think he makes the roster over Fidone, who will begin training camp on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list as he recovers from foot surgery. I think Fidone lands on the practice squad. Wide receiver Locks (5) — Malik Nabers, Darius Slayton, Calvin Austin, Darnell Mooney, Malachi Fields Bubble players (4) — Odell Beckham Jr., JuJu Smith-Schuster, Braxton Berrios, Isaiah Hodgins Long shots (5) — Dalen Cambre, Ryan Miller, Jalin Hyatt, Xavier Gipson, Beaux Collins The Giants got good news when it was reported that Nabers would avoid the PUP list . That doesn’t guarantee that he will be ready Week 1, or that he will be the Nabers of 2024 right away, but it was a positive development. The sixth, and seventh spots at wide receiver, if the Giants keep that many, are wide open. Beckham could get a spot if he makes it through training camp healthy and can practice consistently, but that remains to be seen. If the Giants feel they need special teams contributions from that roster spot, someone like Berrios, Cambre, or Miller could win it. Offensive line Locks (6) — Andrew Thomas, John Michael Schmitz, Francis Mauigoa, Jermaine Eluemunor, Marcus Mbow, Daniel Faalele Bubble players (6) — Jon Runyan, J.C. Davis, Lucas Patrick, Bryan Hudson, Josh Ezeudu, Aaron Stinnie Long shots (4) — Evan Neal, Ryan Schernecke, Jake Kubas, Jarrod Gray (International Exemption) The curveball here is that I have two players enter training camp as reserves (Mbow, Faalele) as locks, and one who is a starter (Runyan) on the bubble. There was little indication throughout spring practices that Runyan’s status as the starting left guard is in jeopardy. There is, though, so much speculation that the Giants could cut Runyan to save $9.25 million in cap space that I have him on the bubble. I will believe there is a competition, though, when I see Faalele, Stinnie, or someone else getting significant first-team reps. Defensive line Locks (4) — D.J. Reader, Darius Alexander, Shelby Harris, Chauncey Golston Bubble players (6) — Bobby Jamison-Travis, Leki Fotu, Zacch Pickens, Sam Roberts, Josh Tupou Long shots (2) — Ben Barten, Anquin Barnes Jr. [ NOTE: Due to his Achilles tendon injury, I did not list Roy Robertson-Harris] I believe Jamison-Travis will make the roster, but want to see him play in pads a few times before I commit to him as a lock. Off-ball linebacker Locks (3) — Arvell Reese, Tremaine Edmunds, Micah McFadden Bubble players (3) — Jack Kelly, Darius Muasau, Zaire Barnes Long shots (0) I think Kelly is making the roster. As a sixth-round pick, though, I can’t list him as a lock before camp begins. Edge defender Locks (3) — Brian Burns, Abdul Carter, Kayvon Thibodeaux Bubble players (1) — Khalid Kareem Long shots (2) — Trace Ford, Caleb Murphy Unless the Giants want to keep someone like Murphy as a special teams player, I think this is how it ends up. Remember, Golston can also play as an edge if needed. Cornerback Locks (4) — Paulson Adebo, Greg Newsome II, Colton Hood, Dru Phillips Bubble players (4) — Deonte Banks, Art Green, Nic Jones, Korie Black Long shots (1) — Jarick Bernard-Converse I debated putting Banks in the “locks” category. Maybe I should have. I do believe he is making the team, especially because of his kickoff return ability. Still, I want to see him carry his good spring through the summer. Safety Locks (3) — Jevon Holland, Tyler Nubin, Ar’Darius Washington Bubble players (2) — Elijah Campbell, Jason Pinnock Long shots (2) — Beau Brade, Raheem Layne The question isn’t really who makes the roster. I think Pinnock and Campbell both end up on the team. The question is going to be whether Washington or Pinnock can steal a starting job, probably from Nubin. Special teams Locks (1) — Jordan Stout (punter) Bubble players (2) — Dominic Zvada (placekicker), Ben Mann (long-snapper) Long shot (1) — Ben Sauls (placekicker) Entering camp, it certainly looks like Zvada and Mann will earn spots on the roster. Totals Locks: 38 I think I was likely a bit conservative in putting players into this category. Bubble players: 28 Long shots: 22 ** After waiving linebacker Cam Jones and defensive tackle C.J. Ravenell on Saturday, the Giants have 89 players on their roster. Jarrod Gray carries an International Exemption, so New York can have 91 players.

title: 5 areas where Jaxson Dart needs to improve, and how the Giants can help him do it
summary: Jaxson Dart did enough in his rookie season to make the New York Giants believe they might have found the answer they have been seeking at quarterback since Eli Manning retired. Dart played well enough, in fact, to be one of the reasons why John Harbaugh was interested in taking the Giants’ head-coaching job. “The […]
full_text: Jaxson Dart | Getty Images Jaxson Dart did enough in his rookie season to make the New York Giants believe they might have found the answer they have been seeking at quarterback since Eli Manning retired. Dart played well enough, in fact, to be one of the reasons why John Harbaugh was interested in taking the Giants’ head-coaching job. “The quarterback’s kind of important. You know, that’s kind of a big deal,” Harbaugh said at his introductory press conference. “I’m excited about Jaxson Dart.” After working with the young quarterback for a few months, Harbaugh’s excitement has grown. “I don’t know about surprised, probably just impressed more than anything. I do think he’s obsessed. I believe he really really wants to be good,” Harbaugh said recently via Bleav in Giants with Bob Papa and Carl Banks. “He’s kinda got the it factor from a leadership standpoint because he’s respected by the guys. They just know how hard he works, how much he prepares and they respect his talent. He’s got some charisma.” Dart has all those things. What he doesn’t have are the pelts on the wall that prove he is a top 10-type quarterback the Giants can and will win with on a consistent basis. Quarterback rankings should be taken with a grain of salt. This list of starting quarterback rankings, though, tells a consistent story: Pro Football Focus — Dart is No. 25 SB Nation — Dart is No. 28 Sports Illustrated — Dart is No. 23 FOX Sports — Dart is No. 21 NBC Sports (Chris Simms) — Dart is No. 22 The story those rankings tell? That Dart has a long way to go to become the quarterback the Giants drafted him to be, and think he can be. Simms summarized Dart this way: Dart is a master of backyard football who can make magic happen but questions remain about the quarterback’s ability to thrive in the pocket heading into his second season. The Giants have been here before Not so long ago a rookie quarterback named Daniel Jones excited the fan base by throwing 24 touchdown passes to 12 interceptions while passing for 3,207 yards in 13 games, 12 of them starts. Jones was “Danny Dimes.” He could throw it. He could run it. His rookie season offered hope that GM Dave Gettleman, criticized for using the No. 6 overall pick in the 2019 NFL Draft on Jones, would be proven right. That, of course, did not happen. Jones has never again reached 20 touchdown passes in a season. The 2025 season with the Indianapolis Colts is the only time Jones has surpassed the 232.8 yards passing per game that he averaged as a rookie. He averaged 238.5 yards in 13 games. So, as good as most feel about Dart’s future, there are no guarantees. The hoped-for leap into the upper tier of quarterbacks never truly happened for Jones. Will it happen for Dart? The New York Post did some Year 2 quarterback research that bodes well for Dart : The Post researched the 33 first-round quarterbacks drafted from 2016-24 to see how many actually took a Year 2 leap — or was it more like a baby step? — and how many went in the other direction. Removing five instances where there is not enough data over the first two seasons to draw a conclusion, 19 of the other 28 experienced a spike in quarterback rating, including seven whose progress was dramatic. Of the nine who went in reverse, only one (the Commanders’ Jayden Daniels) was limited by injury. But perhaps the most interesting finding related to expectations for Dart in 2026 is that quarterbacks who had a new head coach and new offensive coordinator made some of the biggest strides. The Post pointed to Drake Maye of the New England Patriots and Caleb Williams of the Chicago Bears as examples of the quarterback/new coach jump. Young quarterback issues Young quarterbacks in the NFL always have a lot to learn. The variety of things Dart needs to improve upon appear to be things typical of quarterbacks early in their NFL careers. Let’s break these down into a handful of categories. In reality, as you will see, the various categories overlap in some ways. Too much hero ball This is really the “Dart takes too many hits when he runs” category. The Giants can’t take running the ball out of Dart’s game, it is part of what makes him dynamic. Per Sumer Sports, Dart was third in the NFL in quarterback rush yards (487), second in rushing touchdowns (9), and second in Expected Points Added (EPA) when running (38.12). Harbaugh has no intention of taking that away from his quarterback . As has been discussed ad nauseum, what the Giants need Dart to do when he does run is to protect himself, to make smarter decisions about when to put the ball and his body at risk. As a rookie, Dart seemed resistant to the idea that discretion was the better part of valor. The unnecessary hit that he took against the New England Patriots after missing two games with a concussion is evidence of that. The fight that broke out after Patriots LB Christian Elliss hit Jaxson Dart (🎥: @espn ) pic.twitter.com/0vKvKPWRju — Complex Sports (@ComplexSports) December 2, 2025 Offensive coordinator Matt Nagy and quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan have spent time showing Dart clips and going over when it is and is not worth taking risks. Callahan said there have been some “very direct conversations” with Dart about things he needs to improve upon. One of those, of course, is not subjecting himself to unnecessary hits. “There’s an awareness of when to put yourself at risk, when to get out of bounds, when to get down on the ground and not take a hit, and when to be smart with the football,” Callahan said. “Those are things you just point out … but I never want to take that ability to affect the game with his legs because it’s something that makes him a really dangerous player.” Dart sounds like he has gotten the message . “It’s important for the quarterback to make sure how he’s feeling one play that he’s going to feel that same way the next play,” Dart said this spring. “And at the same time, just having the experience last year of sitting out two games, I hadn’t done that in my career. So, I just hated that time of not being out there with my teammates. So obviously I understand the most important thing is to be out there. So, you just grow and learn from things. And I think I’m going to do a good job at it this year for sure. “My competitiveness isn’t going to change at all. I think, just like I said, it just goes into situationally. Just what times it’s worth it and what times it’s not. And just making those mature decisions.” We will see if words lead to actions. Not always making the right read Greg Cosell, one of the premier quarterback analysts in the business, said recently of Dart that “there were times he didn’t see it the right way” during his rookie season. Cosell told Ross Tucker that Dart will “get better in that regard with more experience.” “Jaxson Dart had a solid rookie season…” “There were times he didn't SEE it the right way. And when quarterbacks can run, when they don't see it the right way, they TAKE OFF…” @GregCosell breaks down the Giants QB going into Year 2: pic.twitter.com/AE8YtdXIgj — Ross Tucker Podcast (@RossTuckerPod) July 16, 2026 One of Dart’s strengths is, of course, his ability to make plays with his legs. Cosell pointed out that this is a double-edged sword for young quarterbacks that often causes them to run before they need to. “When quarterbacks can run, when they don’t see it the right way, they take off,” Cosell said. “And that disrupts your pass game and obviously as we saw last year, it caused problems for him in terms of injury.” According to Pro Football Focus, Dart was the worst quarterback in the league last season in terms of allowed pressure — defined as pressures where the quarterback is fully or partly responsible for being pressured while attempting to pass. Dart was at least partly responsible 39.1% of the time when pressured. Shedeur Sanders was second at 27.3%. Dart was at least partially at fault on 50 pressures. Only Maye (52) was responsible for more. Maye’s total,…
